## Poliquin Step Up

`SQU-028 | G1 | Single leg: knee over toes step (VMO) | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Box / bench / step
- **Why we use it:** Low step variations where the knee deliberately travels forward over the toes with the heel raised (Poliquin step up) or from the toes (Patrick step). They load the inner quad and patellar tendon in a controlled way, which is why Poliquin, Ben Patrick and physios use them for knee pain and knee resilience. Small range, huge payoff.
- **Muscles:** Quads (VMO emphasis), knee tendons, ankle
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Stand on a low step, working heel raised on a small plate or wedge (Poliquin) or on the toes (Patrick). 2) Slowly lower the other heel towards the floor by bending the working knee forward over the toes. 3) Lightly tap and drive back up through the front of the foot, keeping the knee in line.
- **Common faults:** Hips shifting back instead of the knee travelling forward; Knee caving inward; Dropping fast instead of controlling the lowering.
- **Progress to:** ATG Split Squat (G2); SSB Split Squat (G2); Split Squat (DB) (G2). **Or progress by:** Higher step, slower tempo, hold DBs, progress to step downs and front foot elevated split squats.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Lower step, hand on the rig, partial range.
- **Same level swaps:** Patrick Step; Petersen Step Up
- **Cautions:** None specific. Knee friendly when kept pain free. Start with a very low step (5 to 10cm) and hand support. Ideal in every knee pain programme.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 20 each leg, slow lowering (3s)
- **Coach sources:** Poliquin, Ben Patrick (ATG), Squat University
- **Also listed in:** Rehab: Knee

## Barbell Split Squat

`SQU-029 | G3 | Single leg: split squat | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Barbell
- **Why we use it:** The entry point of the single leg ladder. A static split stance gives a stable base, so people learn to load one leg at a time safely. It builds balance, fixes imbalances and is far easier on the back than heavy bilateral squats. Front foot elevated adds knee travel (ATG style); cable and landmine versions add stability.
- **This variation:** Barbell: allows the heaviest loading for maximum strength and bone stimulus; earn it with technique (usually G3 to G4, Teams).
- **Muscles:** Quads, glutes, adductors
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Long split stance, both feet pointing forward, hip width apart. 2) Lower the back knee straight down towards the floor. 3) Push through the front foot to stand, keep the torso tall.
- **Common faults:** Stance too narrow (tightrope), losing balance; Front heel lifting; Lunging forward instead of dropping down.
- **Progress to:** Barbell RFESS (G4); Paused RFESS (G4); 1.5 Rep RFESS (G4). **Or progress by:** Add load, elevate the front foot (ATG style), then elevate the back foot (RFESS).
- **Regress to:** ATG Split Squat (G2); SSB Split Squat (G2); Split Squat (DB) (G2). **Or regress by:** TRX or rig assisted split squat, shorter range, isometric split squat hold.
- **Same level swaps:** Band Resisted Split Squat; Offset Single Arm Split Squat
- **Cautions:** None specific. Knee friendly when depth is controlled. Use a pad under the back knee. Hold a support for balance in seniors.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 (each leg)
- **Coach sources:** Boyle, Squat University, Ben Patrick (front foot elevated)

## Box Pistol Squat

`SQU-032 | G3 | Single leg squat (advanced) | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Box / bench / step
- **Why we use it:** Single leg squats are the top of Mike Boyle's single leg ladder: maximum leg strength with minimal spinal load, and they expose left/right imbalances. Box versions control depth so they are accessible far earlier than a full pistol.
- **Muscles:** Quads, glutes, adductors, balance and foot control
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Stand on one leg, other leg held forward (pistol) or behind (skater/shrimp). 2) Sit back and down slowly to the box or depth target, knee over the middle of the foot. 3) Drive up through the whole foot without the knee caving.
- **Common faults:** Knee diving inward; Collapsing onto the box; Heel lifting.
- **Progress to:** Single Leg Box Squat (G4); Single Leg Squat to Bench (G4). **Or progress by:** Lower the box, remove support, add a light counterweight held forward, then load.
- **Regress to:** Low Box Step Down (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Forward Step Down (G2). **Or regress by:** Higher box, TRX assisted, step downs, split squat.
- **Same level swaps:** Pistol Squat; Skater Squat; Shrimp Squat
- **Cautions:** Knee. Demanding on the knee. Use a box and TRX support first. Not for acute knee pain or early post surgery.
- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 5 to 8 each leg, slow lowering
- **Coach sources:** Boyle, Squat University, Gambetta

`SQU-037 | G1 | Single leg: split squat isometric | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Holding the bottom of a split squat builds strength and tendon tolerance at the exact point people are weakest, with very low joint irritation. Great for knee pain, beginners and as a pre-lift primer.
- **This variation:** Isometric: builds strength and tendon tolerance in a fixed position with minimal joint irritation.
- **Muscles:** Quads, glutes, hip flexors
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Get into a split squat with both knees around 90 degrees. 2) Back knee hovering just off the floor. 3) Hold, breathe, push the front foot into the floor.
- **Common faults:** Leaning on the front thigh; Front knee caving; Holding the breath.
- **Progress to:** TRX Lunge (G2); DB Step Up (G2); Lunge Pulses (G2). **Or progress by:** Hold longer, hold DBs, progress to dynamic split squats.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Higher position, hand support.
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very knee friendly. Raise the back knee position if painful.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 5 x 20 to 45s holds, rest 60s, about 70% effort each leg
- **Coach sources:** Rehab research (isometrics), Squat University
- **Also listed in:** Rehab: Knee

## Skater Squat

`SQU-038 | G3 | Single leg squat (advanced) | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Single leg squats are the top of Mike Boyle's single leg ladder: maximum leg strength with minimal spinal load, and they expose left/right imbalances. Box versions control depth so they are accessible far earlier than a full pistol.
- **Muscles:** Quads, glutes, adductors, balance and foot control
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Stand on one leg, other leg held forward (pistol) or behind (skater/shrimp). 2) Sit back and down slowly to the box or depth target, knee over the middle of the foot. 3) Drive up through the whole foot without the knee caving.
- **Common faults:** Knee diving inward; Collapsing onto the box; Heel lifting.
- **Progress to:** Single Leg Box Squat (G4); Single Leg Squat to Bench (G4). **Or progress by:** Lower the box, remove support, add a light counterweight held forward, then load.
- **Regress to:** Low Box Step Down (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Forward Step Down (G2). **Or regress by:** Higher box, TRX assisted, step downs, split squat.
- **Same level swaps:** Pistol Squat; Shrimp Squat; Box Pistol Squat
- **Cautions:** Knee. Demanding on the knee. Use a box and TRX support first. Not for acute knee pain or early post surgery.
- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 5 to 8 each leg, slow lowering
- **Coach sources:** Boyle, Squat University, Gambetta

## Reverse Lunge (Bodyweight)

`SQU-039 | G1 | Single leg: reverse lunge | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Stepping backwards keeps the shin more vertical, so it is far kinder to the knees than forward lunges while still training single leg strength and balance. The default lunge at Optimal. Deficit and slider versions increase range and control.
- **Muscles:** Quads, glutes, hamstrings
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Stand tall, step one foot back. 2) Drop the back knee towards the floor, front shin fairly vertical. 3) Drive through the front heel to stand back up.
- **Common faults:** Stepping too short; Front knee collapsing; Leaning forward and rounding.
- **Progress to:** SSB Reverse Lunge (G2); Reverse Lunge (DB) (G2); Cable Reverse Lunge (G2). **Or progress by:** Add load, deficit (front foot on a plate), knee drive at the top, barbell/landmine.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Split squat (static), hand support, shorter range.
- **Same level swaps:** Split Squat (Supported); Split Squat (Bodyweight); TRX Assisted Split Squat
- **Cautions:** None specific. Most knee friendly lunge. Use a pad and hand support for beginners.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 (each leg)
- **Coach sources:** Boyle, Cosgrove, Squat University

## Bulgarian Split Squat Jump (Light)

`SQU-044 | G2 | Power: jumps, hops and landings (plyometric) | HYBRID | Group: No | Impact: high | Teams only: Yes | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Box / bench / step
- **Why we use it:** Jumps and hops train power, tendon stiffness and bone (impact is a key bone stimulus in LIFTMOR). Landings (snap downs, drop squats, jump and stick) teach the body to absorb force, the foundation of injury prevention. Progress carefully: landing before jumping, low before high, two legs before one.
- **This variation:** Reduced range/load version: used for rehab, beginners, warm ups or flare up days.
- **Muscles:** Whole lower body, tendons, nervous system
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Land softly and quietly, hips back, knees over toes. 2) Stick the landing for a second before the next rep. 3) Quality over quantity: stop when height or control drops.
- **Common faults:** Landing stiff legged or with knees caving; Too many reps (plyos are not cardio); Progressing too fast.
- **Progress to:** A Skip (G3); Box Jump (G3); Bounding (G3). **Or progress by:** Landings → small jumps → box jumps → broad jumps → single leg hops → depth jumps.
- **Regress to:** Poliquin Step Up (G1); Petersen Step Up (G1); Split Squat (Bodyweight) (G1). **Or regress by:** Snap downs/drop squat and stick, step ups, sled push, med ball throws.
- **Same level swaps:** Snap Downs; Drop Squat; Pogo Hops (Low)
- **Cautions:** Knee, Low back, Osteoporosis/osteopenia, Pelvic floor. IMPACT: excluded from Optimal GROUP sessions (no jumping rule). Teams only after screening. Avoid with pelvic floor symptoms, osteoporosis with fracture history, joint replacements, acute knee/Achilles pain.
- **Group swap:** Group swap (no jumping): sled push, fast step ups, med ball chest pass or slam, KB swing, fast sit to stand
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 5 sets x 3 to 6 reps, full recovery (60 to 120s), stop when speed drops; 2 to 3 sessions/week max, low total contacts (20 to 60)
- **Coach sources:** Gambetta, DeFranco (dynamic effort), LIFTMOR research (impact for bone)

## Curtsy Lunge

`SQU-046 | G2 | Single leg: lunge (rotational/adductor bias) | HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Stepping back and across challenges the hips in a different plane, hitting the side glutes and inner thighs. Good variety and good for hip stability and golf.
- **Muscles:** Glutes (especially glute med), adductors, quads
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Step one foot back and across behind the other. 2) Lower straight down with the front knee tracking the toes. 3) Push through the front foot to return.
- **Common faults:** Twisting the hips excessively; Front knee caving; Losing balance from too narrow a step.
- **Progress to:** Goblet RFESS (G3); Pistol Squat (G3); Skater Squat (G3). **Or progress by:** Add load, deficit, pair with a single leg RDL.
- **Regress to:** Poliquin Step Up (G1); Petersen Step Up (G1); Split Squat (Bodyweight) (G1). **Or regress by:** Shorter range, hand support, reverse lunge.
- **Same level swaps:** Curtsy Lunge (DB)
- **Cautions:** Knee. Can irritate knees and hips if the range is forced. Keep it pain free.
- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9 (each side)
- **Coach sources:** Gambetta (multi plane), Cosgrove

## Offset Single Arm Split Squat

`SQU-048 | G3 | Single leg: split squat | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** The entry point of the single leg ladder. A static split stance gives a stable base, so people learn to load one leg at a time safely. It builds balance, fixes imbalances and is far easier on the back than heavy bilateral squats. Front foot elevated adds knee travel (ATG style); cable and landmine versions add stability.
- **This variation:** One sided loading adds an anti rotation / anti lateral flexion core challenge and exposes left/right differences.
- **Muscles:** Quads, glutes, adductors
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Long split stance, both feet pointing forward, hip width apart. 2) Lower the back knee straight down towards the floor. 3) Push through the front foot to stand, keep the torso tall.
- **Common faults:** Stance too narrow (tightrope), losing balance; Front heel lifting; Lunging forward instead of dropping down.
- **Progress to:** Paused RFESS (G4); Barbell RFESS (G4); 1.5 Rep RFESS (G4). **Or progress by:** Add load, elevate the front foot (ATG style), then elevate the back foot (RFESS).
- **Regress to:** ATG Split Squat (G2); SSB Split Squat (G2); Split Squat (DB) (G2). **Or regress by:** TRX or rig assisted split squat, shorter range, isometric split squat hold.
- **Same level swaps:** Barbell Split Squat; Band Resisted Split Squat
- **Cautions:** None specific. Knee friendly when depth is controlled. Use a pad under the back knee. Hold a support for balance in seniors.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 (each leg)
- **Coach sources:** Boyle, Squat University, Ben Patrick (front foot elevated)

## Forward Lunge (DB)

`SQU-053 | G2 | Single leg: forward / walking lunge | BURN, HYBRID, STRONG | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Dumbbells (confirm)
- **Why we use it:** Forward and walking lunges add deceleration and balance: you have to control the body moving forward over the front leg. Very functional and very metabolic, so they suit BURN and HYBRID sessions. Loaded carry lunges add grip and core.
- **Muscles:** Quads, glutes, hamstrings, balance, grip when loaded
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Long step forward, land heel first. 2) Drop the back knee down, front knee over the middle of the foot. 3) Push through the front foot and step through to the next rep.
- **Common faults:** Short choppy steps that load the front knee; Front knee caving; Torso collapsing forward.
- **Progress to:** Barbell Walking Lunge (G3); Overhead Walking Lunge (KB) (G3); Overhead Walking Lunge (Plate) (G3). **Or progress by:** Add load (DB, KB rack, overhead), pulses, longer distance.
- **Regress to:** Split Squat (Supported) (G1); Split Squat (Bodyweight) (G1); TRX Assisted Split Squat (G1). **Or regress by:** Reverse lunge, split squat, hand support.
- **Same level swaps:** Walking Lunge (DB); Suitcase Lunge Carry; TRX Lunge
- **Cautions:** Knee. More knee stress than reverse lunges. Swap to reverse lunges or split squats with knee pain. Needs space in groups.
- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9 (each leg) or 20 to 30m
- **Coach sources:** Gambetta (lunge matrix), Cosgrove, Paul Chek (lunge pattern)

- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 5 to 8 each leg, slow lowering
- **Coach sources:** Boyle, Squat University, Gambetta

## Walking Lunge (DB)

`SQU-055 | G2 | Single leg: forward / walking lunge | BURN, HYBRID, STRONG | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Dumbbells (confirm)
- **Why we use it:** Forward and walking lunges add deceleration and balance: you have to control the body moving forward over the front leg. Very functional and very metabolic, so they suit BURN and HYBRID sessions. Loaded carry lunges add grip and core.
- **Muscles:** Quads, glutes, hamstrings, balance, grip when loaded
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Long step forward, land heel first. 2) Drop the back knee down, front knee over the middle of the foot. 3) Push through the front foot and step through to the next rep.
- **Common faults:** Short choppy steps that load the front knee; Front knee caving; Torso collapsing forward.
- **Progress to:** Barbell Walking Lunge (G3); Overhead Walking Lunge (KB) (G3); Overhead Walking Lunge (Plate) (G3). **Or progress by:** Add load (DB, KB rack, overhead), pulses, longer distance.
- **Regress to:** Split Squat (Supported) (G1); Split Squat (Bodyweight) (G1); TRX Assisted Split Squat (G1). **Or regress by:** Reverse lunge, split squat, hand support.
- **Same level swaps:** Forward Lunge (DB); Suitcase Lunge Carry; TRX Lunge
- **Cautions:** Knee. More knee stress than reverse lunges. Swap to reverse lunges or split squats with knee pain. Needs space in groups.
- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9 (each leg) or 20 to 30m
- **Coach sources:** Gambetta (lunge matrix), Cosgrove, Paul Chek (lunge pattern)

## Front Rack Reverse Lunge (Barbell)

`SQU-056 | G3 | Single leg: reverse lunge | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Barbell
- **Why we use it:** Stepping backwards keeps the shin more vertical, so it is far kinder to the knees than forward lunges while still training single leg strength and balance. The default lunge at Optimal. Deficit and slider versions increase range and control.
- **This variation:** Barbell: allows the heaviest loading for maximum strength and bone stimulus; earn it with technique (usually G3 to G4, Teams).
- **Muscles:** Quads, glutes, hamstrings
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Stand tall, step one foot back. 2) Drop the back knee towards the floor, front shin fairly vertical. 3) Drive through the front heel to stand back up.
- **Common faults:** Stepping too short; Front knee collapsing; Leaning forward and rounding.
- **Progress to:** Barbell RFESS (G4); Paused RFESS (G4); 1.5 Rep RFESS (G4). **Or progress by:** Add load, deficit (front foot on a plate), knee drive at the top, barbell/landmine.
- **Regress to:** Reverse Lunge to RDL (G2); SSB Reverse Lunge (G2); Reverse Lunge (DB) (G2). **Or regress by:** Split squat (static), hand support, shorter range.
- **Same level swaps:** Barbell Reverse Lunge; Slider Reverse Lunge; Deficit Reverse Lunge
- **Cautions:** None specific. Most knee friendly lunge. Use a pad and hand support for beginners.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 (each leg)
- **Coach sources:** Boyle, Cosgrove, Squat University

## Walking Lunge Front Rack (KB)

## Shrimp Squat

`SQU-058 | G3 | Single leg squat (advanced) | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Single leg squats are the top of Mike Boyle's single leg ladder: maximum leg strength with minimal spinal load, and they expose left/right imbalances. Box versions control depth so they are accessible far earlier than a full pistol.
- **Muscles:** Quads, glutes, adductors, balance and foot control
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Stand on one leg, other leg held forward (pistol) or behind (skater/shrimp). 2) Sit back and down slowly to the box or depth target, knee over the middle of the foot. 3) Drive up through the whole foot without the knee caving.
- **Common faults:** Knee diving inward; Collapsing onto the box; Heel lifting.
- **Progress to:** Single Leg Box Squat (G4); Single Leg Squat to Bench (G4). **Or progress by:** Lower the box, remove support, add a light counterweight held forward, then load.
- **Regress to:** Low Box Step Down (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Forward Step Down (G2). **Or regress by:** Higher box, TRX assisted, step downs, split squat.
- **Same level swaps:** Pistol Squat; Skater Squat; Box Pistol Squat
- **Cautions:** Knee. Demanding on the knee. Use a box and TRX support first. Not for acute knee pain or early post surgery.
- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 5 to 8 each leg, slow lowering
- **Coach sources:** Boyle, Squat University, Gambetta

# 03. HINGE PATTERN: BILATERAL

*Hip dominant, both feet*

**Grade ladder at a glance** (use this to slot every member into the same session at their level):

- **G1**: Hip Hinge Dowel Drill, Bodyweight Good Morning, KB Deadlift, DB Deadlift, Glute Bridge, Glute Bridge (Mini Band), Sumo KB Deadlift, Hip Thrust (Bodyweight), Elevated KB Deadlift, Hip Thrust (DB), Banded Hip Thrust, Frog Pump, B Stance Hip Thrust, Swiss Ball Bridge, Nordic Curl (Assisted), Cable Pull Through, Band Pull Through, Dead Bug Bridge Hold, Landmine Deadlift
- **G2**: KB Swing (Two Hand), KB Swing (Hip Height), KB Dead Stop Swing, American KB Swing, DB Romanian Deadlift, KB Romanian Deadlift, Double KB Deadlift, Weighted Glute Bridge (DB), Barbell Glute Bridge, Tempo DB RDL, Barbell Hip Thrust, Paused Hip Thrust, Trap Bar Deadlift (High Handles), Trap Bar RDL, Swiss Ball Hamstring Curl, TRX Hamstring Curl, Reverse Hyper (Bench), 45 Degree Back Extension, Snatch Grip RDL, Back Extension (Hold Plate), Cable Romanian Deadlift, Seated Good Morning, Banded Good Morning, Landmine Romanian Deadlift
- **G3**: Double KB Romanian Deadlift, Paused DB RDL, Trap Bar Deadlift, Barbell Romanian Deadlift, Slider Hamstring Curl, Barbell Good Morning, Hang Clean Pull, Double KB Swing
- **G4**: Barbell Deadlift ✱, Sumo Deadlift ✱, Block Pull ✱, Rack Pull ✱, Paused Deadlift ✱, Deficit Deadlift ✱, Jefferson Curl (Light) ✱, Clean Pull (Barbell) ✱, Snatch Grip Deadlift ✱

✱ = not for group sessions (impact).

## Hip Hinge Dowel Drill

`HGB-001 | G1 | Hinge: pattern teaching | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Dowel (confirm)
- **Why we use it:** Teaches people to move at the hips not the spine. The dowel gives instant feedback (head, upper back and tailbone stay in contact). Every hinge exercise depends on this skill, so McGill and Squat University teach it first.
- **Muscles:** Hamstrings, glutes, spinal control
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Dowel along the spine touching head, upper back and tailbone. 2) Soft knees, push the hips back as if closing a car door with your bum. 3) Hinge until you feel the hamstrings, keep all three contact points, stand back up.
- **Common faults:** Losing the dowel contact at the low back; Bending the knees into a squat; Looking up and cranking the neck.
- **Progress to:** Double KB Deadlift (G2); Single Arm Cable Pull Through (G2). **Or progress by:** Hold a KB at the chest, progress to KB deadlift from blocks.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Hinge to a wall (bum touches the wall) with a smaller range.
- **Same level swaps:** KB Deadlift; DB Deadlift; Donkey Kick
- **Cautions:** None specific. Ideal for back pain members. No load, no risk.
- **Default prescription:** 2 sets x 8 to 10 slow reps (warm up)
- **Coach sources:** McGill, Squat University, Dan John
- **Also listed in:** Rehab: Hip, Rehab: Lower Back

## KB Swing (Two Hand)

`HGB-002 | G2 | Hinge: ballistic (power) | BURN, HYBRID, STRONG | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Kettlebell
- **Why we use it:** The king of hinge conditioning (Dan John, Pavel). Trains explosive hip extension (power) and heart rate at the same time with no impact on the knees. Excellent for fat loss, posture and glute strength. Dead stop versions teach control; single arm versions add anti rotation.
- **Muscles:** Glutes, hamstrings, core, grip, cardiovascular system
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Hike the bell back high between the thighs. 2) Snap the hips forward, squeeze the glutes, let the bell float to chest height. 3) Let it fall, hinge late, keep the spine neutral.
- **Common faults:** Squatting the swing instead of hinging; Lifting with the arms; Leaning back at the top.
- **Progress to:** Double KB Swing (G3); Single Arm KB Swing (G3); Single Arm KB Swing to Catch (G3). **Or progress by:** Heavier bell, single arm, alternating, swings EMOM, heavier with fewer reps for power.
- **Regress to:** KB Deadlift (G1); Sumo KB Deadlift (G1); Elevated KB Deadlift (G1). **Or regress by:** KB deadlift, dead stop swing, lighter bell, cable pull through.
- **Same level swaps:** KB Swings; KB Swing (Power); American KB Swing
- **Cautions:** Low back. Back friendly when the hinge is good. Teach the KB deadlift first. Not for acute low back pain. American (overhead) swings stress shoulders and low back: use hip height swings instead.
- **Default prescription:** 4 to 10 sets x 10 to 20 reps, or EMOM; 'hike, snap, float'
- **Coach sources:** Dan John, Pavel Tsatsouline, Cosgrove

## Bodyweight Good Morning

`HGB-003 | G1 | Hinge: good morning | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Barbell
- **Why we use it:** Load sits on the upper back while the hips hinge, which strengthens the hamstrings and back extensors. Bodyweight and banded versions are great hinge teaching tools; barbell versions are advanced. ATG style seated good mornings build hamstring and back mobility.
- **Muscles:** Hamstrings, glutes, spinal erectors
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Soft knees, brace, push the hips back. 2) Keep the spine long and neutral. 3) Stand up by driving the hips forward.
- **Common faults:** Rounding the spine; Bending the knees too much; Going deeper than hamstring length allows.
- **Progress to:** SSB Good Morning (G2); Seated Good Morning (G2); Banded Good Morning (G2). **Or progress by:** Band → light barbell → SSB good morning, tempo, pause.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Bodyweight, dowel hinge drill.
- **Same level swaps:** Hip Hinge to Wall; Hip Hinge Dowel Drill
- **Cautions:** Low back. Loaded good mornings are not for low back pain. Keep loads light and range controlled for 40+.
- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9
- **Coach sources:** Westside/DeFranco, Ben Patrick (seated), Poliquin

## KB Deadlift

`HGB-005 | G1 | Hinge: deadlift (KB/DB/landmine) | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Kettlebell
- **Why we use it:** The safest way to teach lifting from the floor. Picking things up is a life skill (Primal Pattern 'bend'). Raising the bell on blocks reduces range for beginners and back pain; suitcase versions add anti lateral flexion.
- **Muscles:** Glutes, hamstrings, back, grip
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Bell between the feet (or beside for suitcase), hinge down with a flat back. 2) Grip, pull the shoulders down, brace. 3) Push the floor away and stand tall, squeeze the glutes.
- **Common faults:** Squatting down too low; Rounding to reach the bell; Leaning back at the top.
- **Progress to:** KB Swings (G2); KB Swing (Power) (G2); American KB Swing (G2). **Or progress by:** Heavier bell, double KB, lower to the floor, progress to RDL, swing and trap bar.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Bell on a block/step, hinge drill.
- **Same level swaps:** Sumo KB Deadlift; Elevated KB Deadlift; KB Deadlift (Elevated)
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very back friendly. Elevate the bell on a step for limited hip mobility or back history.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8
- **Coach sources:** Dan John, McGill, Cosgrove

## DB Romanian Deadlift

`HGB-009 | G2 | Hinge: Romanian deadlift | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Dumbbells (confirm)
- **Why we use it:** The RDL starts from the top and lowers the weight by pushing the hips back, so it builds hamstrings and glutes in a lengthened position with low skill demand. It's the best hamstring builder for most members and a staple for posture and back resilience.
- **Muscles:** Hamstrings, glutes, spinal erectors, grip
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Soft knees, weight close to the legs. 2) Push the hips back, slide the weight down the thighs, keep the back flat. 3) Stop when the hamstrings are tight (usually mid shin), drive the hips forward to stand.
- **Common faults:** Rounding the back to go lower; Squatting it by bending the knees too much; Weight drifting away from the legs.
- **Progress to:** Paused DB RDL (G3); Barbell Romanian Deadlift (G3); Double KB Romanian Deadlift (G3). **Or progress by:** DB → double KB → trap bar → barbell RDL, tempo (4s lowering), pauses, deficit.
- **Regress to:** DB Deadlift (G1); KB Deadlift (G1); Sumo KB Deadlift (G1). **Or regress by:** KB deadlift from blocks, cable pull through, hinge dowel drill, reduce range.
- **Same level swaps:** Tempo DB RDL; Trap Bar RDL; Snatch Grip RDL
- **Cautions:** None specific. Back friendly with good form and controlled range. Reduce range for tight hamstrings or low back sensitivity.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8
- **Coach sources:** Poliquin, Cosgrove, DeFranco

## Glute Bridge

`HGB-010 | G1 | Hinge: hip extension (bridge / thrust) | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Bridges and hip thrusts train the glutes at their strongest point (full hip extension) with almost no spinal load. They are essential for back pain, knee pain, posture, sprinting and golf power, and are safe for nearly everyone. Single leg versions fix imbalances.
- **Muscles:** Glutes, hamstrings
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Feet flat, shins vertical at the top. 2) Tuck the ribs down, drive through the heels and squeeze the glutes to lift. 3) Pause at the top without arching the low back, lower slowly.
- **Common faults:** Arching the low back instead of extending the hips; Feet too far away (all hamstrings); Pushing through the toes.
- **Progress to:** Paused Hip Thrust (G2); Barbell Hip Thrust (G2); Hip Thrust (Paused) (G2). **Or progress by:** Bridge → hip thrust off a bench → load (DB, barbell) → single leg, add pauses or bands.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Floor bridge, shorter range, isometric hold.
- **Same level swaps:** Frog Pump; Hip Thrust (DB); Banded Hip Thrust
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very joint friendly. Use a pad on the hips when loaded. Shoulder elevated versions need a stable bench.
- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9 (pause 1 to 2s at the top)
- **Coach sources:** Cosgrove, McGill, Boyle
- **Also listed in:** Rehab: Hip, Rehab: Knee, Rehab: Lower Back, Mobility And Warm Up

## KB Romanian Deadlift

`HGB-011 | G2 | Hinge: Romanian deadlift | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Kettlebell
- **Why we use it:** The RDL starts from the top and lowers the weight by pushing the hips back, so it builds hamstrings and glutes in a lengthened position with low skill demand. It's the best hamstring builder for most members and a staple for posture and back resilience.
- **Muscles:** Hamstrings, glutes, spinal erectors, grip
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Soft knees, weight close to the legs. 2) Push the hips back, slide the weight down the thighs, keep the back flat. 3) Stop when the hamstrings are tight (usually mid shin), drive the hips forward to stand.
- **Common faults:** Rounding the back to go lower; Squatting it by bending the knees too much; Weight drifting away from the legs.
- **Progress to:** Double KB Romanian Deadlift (G3); Paused DB RDL (G3); Barbell Romanian Deadlift (G3). **Or progress by:** DB → double KB → trap bar → barbell RDL, tempo (4s lowering), pauses, deficit.
- **Regress to:** KB Deadlift (G1); Sumo KB Deadlift (G1); Elevated KB Deadlift (G1). **Or regress by:** KB deadlift from blocks, cable pull through, hinge dowel drill, reduce range.
- **Same level swaps:** Tempo DB RDL; Trap Bar RDL; Snatch Grip RDL
- **Cautions:** None specific. Back friendly with good form and controlled range. Reduce range for tight hamstrings or low back sensitivity.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8
- **Coach sources:** Poliquin, Cosgrove, DeFranco

## Glute Bridge (Mini Band)

`HGB-012 | G1 | Hinge: hip extension (bridge / thrust) | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

## Double KB Deadlift

`HGB-013 | G2 | Hinge: deadlift (KB/DB/landmine) | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Kettlebell
- **Why we use it:** The safest way to teach lifting from the floor. Picking things up is a life skill (Primal Pattern 'bend'). Raising the bell on blocks reduces range for beginners and back pain; suitcase versions add anti lateral flexion.
- **This variation:** Double KB: heavier total load plus a front rack or bilateral grip demand.
- **Muscles:** Glutes, hamstrings, back, grip
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Bell between the feet (or beside for suitcase), hinge down with a flat back. 2) Grip, pull the shoulders down, brace. 3) Push the floor away and stand tall, squeeze the glutes.
- **Common faults:** Squatting down too low; Rounding to reach the bell; Leaning back at the top.
- **Progress to:** Double KB Swing (G3); Single Arm KB Swing (G3); Double KB Romanian Deadlift (G3). **Or progress by:** Heavier bell, double KB, lower to the floor, progress to RDL, swing and trap bar.
- **Regress to:** KB Deadlift (G1); Sumo KB Deadlift (G1); Elevated KB Deadlift (G1). **Or regress by:** Bell on a block/step, hinge drill.
- **Same level swaps:** KB Swings; KB Swing (Power); American KB Swing
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very back friendly. Elevate the bell on a step for limited hip mobility or back history.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8
- **Coach sources:** Dan John, McGill, Cosgrove

## Double KB Romanian Deadlift

`HGB-015 | G3 | Hinge: Romanian deadlift | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Kettlebell
- **Why we use it:** The RDL starts from the top and lowers the weight by pushing the hips back, so it builds hamstrings and glutes in a lengthened position with low skill demand. It's the best hamstring builder for most members and a staple for posture and back resilience.
- **This variation:** Double KB: heavier total load plus a front rack or bilateral grip demand.
- **Muscles:** Hamstrings, glutes, spinal erectors, grip
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Soft knees, weight close to the legs. 2) Push the hips back, slide the weight down the thighs, keep the back flat. 3) Stop when the hamstrings are tight (usually mid shin), drive the hips forward to stand.
- **Common faults:** Rounding the back to go lower; Squatting it by bending the knees too much; Weight drifting away from the legs.
- **Progress to:** Offset KB Single Leg RDL (G4). **Or progress by:** DB → double KB → trap bar → barbell RDL, tempo (4s lowering), pauses, deficit.
- **Regress to:** KB Romanian Deadlift (G2); Tempo DB RDL (G2); Trap Bar RDL (G2). **Or regress by:** KB deadlift from blocks, cable pull through, hinge dowel drill, reduce range.
- **Same level swaps:** Paused DB RDL; Barbell Romanian Deadlift
- **Cautions:** None specific. Back friendly with good form and controlled range. Reduce range for tight hamstrings or low back sensitivity.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8
- **Coach sources:** Poliquin, Cosgrove, DeFranco

## Trap Bar Deadlift

`HGB-025 | G3 | Hinge: trap bar deadlift | STRONG | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Trap bar (confirm)
- **Why we use it:** The trap bar lets people stand inside the weight with neutral grip, so the load sits in line with the body. Far less low back stress than a straight bar and much easier to learn. DeFranco and Cosgrove's go to heavy lift and Optimal's default heavy deadlift for 40+ (bone density, strength, grip).
- **Muscles:** Glutes, quads, hamstrings, back, grip
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Stand in the middle, hinge down and grip the handles. 2) Chest proud, take the slack out of the bar, brace. 3) Push the floor away, stand tall, lower with control.
- **Common faults:** Hips shooting up first; Rounding the back off the floor; Jerking the bar off the floor.
- **Progress to:** Rack Pull (G4); Block Pull (G4); Sumo Deadlift (G4). **Or progress by:** Add load, low handles, pause just off the floor, rep max progressions (Teams G4).
- **Regress to:** Trap Bar RDL (G2); Trap Bar Deadlift (High Handles) (G2); Tempo DB RDL (G2). **Or regress by:** High handles, KB deadlift from blocks, lighter load.
- **Same level swaps:** Trap Bar Deadlift (Low Handles); Paused DB RDL; Barbell Romanian Deadlift
- **Cautions:** None specific. The most joint friendly heavy lift. High handles reduce range for tall members or stiff hips/backs.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8
- **Coach sources:** DeFranco, Cosgrove, LIFTMOR research

- **Progress to:** Paused Hip Thrust (G2); Barbell Hip Thrust (G2); Hip Thrust (Paused) (G2). **Or progress by:** Bridge → hip thrust off a bench → load (DB, barbell) → single leg, add pauses or bands.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Floor bridge, shorter range, isometric hold.
- **Same level swaps:** Glute Bridge; Hip Thrust (DB); Banded Hip Thrust
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very joint friendly. Use a pad on the hips when loaded. Shoulder elevated versions need a stable bench.
- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9 (pause 1 to 2s at the top)
- **Coach sources:** Cosgrove, McGill, Boyle
- **Also listed in:** Rehab: Hip

## Trap Bar RDL

`HGB-029 | G2 | Hinge: Romanian deadlift | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Trap bar (confirm)
- **Why we use it:** The RDL starts from the top and lowers the weight by pushing the hips back, so it builds hamstrings and glutes in a lengthened position with low skill demand. It's the best hamstring builder for most members and a staple for posture and back resilience.
- **Muscles:** Hamstrings, glutes, spinal erectors, grip
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Soft knees, weight close to the legs. 2) Push the hips back, slide the weight down the thighs, keep the back flat. 3) Stop when the hamstrings are tight (usually mid shin), drive the hips forward to stand.
- **Common faults:** Rounding the back to go lower; Squatting it by bending the knees too much; Weight drifting away from the legs.
- **Progress to:** Paused DB RDL (G3); Barbell Romanian Deadlift (G3); Double KB Romanian Deadlift (G3). **Or progress by:** DB → double KB → trap bar → barbell RDL, tempo (4s lowering), pauses, deficit.
- **Regress to:** KB Deadlift (G1); DB Deadlift (G1); Sumo KB Deadlift (G1). **Or regress by:** KB deadlift from blocks, cable pull through, hinge dowel drill, reduce range.
- **Same level swaps:** Tempo DB RDL; Snatch Grip RDL; DB Romanian Deadlift
- **Cautions:** None specific. Back friendly with good form and controlled range. Reduce range for tight hamstrings or low back sensitivity.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8
- **Coach sources:** Poliquin, Cosgrove, DeFranco

## Barbell Deadlift

`HGB-031 | G4 | Hinge: barbell deadlift | STRONG | Group: No | Impact: none | Teams only: Yes | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Barbell
- **Why we use it:** The heaviest total body strength lift. Builds posterior chain strength, grip and bone density (LIFTMOR). Block and rack pulls shorten the range for beginners or back sensitivity; deficit and paused versions are advanced.
- **This variation:** Barbell: allows the heaviest loading for maximum strength and bone stimulus; earn it with technique (usually G3 to G4, Teams).
- **Muscles:** Glutes, hamstrings, back, grip, whole body
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Bar over the middle of the foot, shins close. 2) Grip, chest up, pull the slack out, brace hard. 3) Push the floor away, bar stays close, lock out with the glutes.
- **Common faults:** Rounding the back; Bar drifting away from the legs; Hyperextending at the top.
- **Progress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or progress by:** Add load, pause off the floor, deficit, rep max progressions.
- **Regress to:** Barbell Romanian Deadlift (G3); Paused DB RDL (G3); Trap Bar Deadlift (G3). **Or regress by:** Block/rack pull, trap bar deadlift, KB deadlift.
- **Same level swaps:** Rack Pull; Block Pull; Sumo Deadlift
- **Cautions:** Low back, Pelvic floor. Highest low back demand. Not for active back pain. Trap bar is the default for most 40+ members. Teams G4 only for straight bar.
- **Group swap:** Teams only (heavy or high skill): in groups use a G3 regression from the Regress to list
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8
- **Coach sources:** DeFranco, LIFTMOR research, Poliquin

## Swiss Ball Hamstring Curl

`HGB-032 | G2 | Hinge: knee flexion (hamstring curl) | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Swiss ball (confirm)
- **Why we use it:** Hamstrings both extend the hip and bend the knee; curls train the knee bending role that RDLs miss. Strong hamstrings protect knees and reduce hamstring strain risk. Nordic curls are among the best researched injury prevention exercises.
- **This variation:** Swiss ball adds instability for core control (Paul Chek); keep loads modest.
- **Muscles:** Hamstrings (knee flexion function), glutes
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Lie on your back, heels on the ball/sliders/TRX, lift the hips. 2) Curl the heels towards the bum keeping the hips high. 3) Extend slowly back out (control is the exercise).
- **Common faults:** Hips dropping during the curl; Rushing the lowering; Cramping (start with fewer reps).
- **Progress to:** Single Leg Swiss Ball Curl (G3); Nordic Curl (Full) (G3); Slider Hamstring Curl (G3). **Or progress by:** Hips stay up throughout, single leg, slower lowering, Nordic progression.
- **Regress to:** Swiss Ball Bridge (G1); Frog Pump (G1); Glute Bridge (G1). **Or regress by:** Hips on the floor curl, eccentric only, double leg.
- **Same level swaps:** Hamstring Curl (Swiss Ball); TRX Hamstring Curl
- **Cautions:** None specific. Knee friendly. Nordics are demanding: use band assistance and partial range, expect soreness at first.
- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9
- **Coach sources:** Squat University, Ben Patrick (Nordic), Poliquin

## Reverse Hyper (Bench)

`HGB-042 | G2 | Hinge: back extension | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Box / bench / step
- **Why we use it:** Strengthens the back extensors and glutes, improving posture and back resilience. Reverse hypers decompress the spine as they train. Extend to neutral only: the goal is a strong, straight spine, not arching.
- **Muscles:** Spinal erectors, glutes, hamstrings
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Hinge at the hips, keep the spine long. 2) Lift to a straight line from head to heels using the glutes. 3) Lower with control.
- **Common faults:** Hyperextending at the top; Swinging/using momentum; Rounding heavily at the bottom under load.
- **Progress to:** Paused DB RDL (G3); Hang Clean Pull (G3); Double KB Swing (G3). **Or progress by:** Hold a plate, single leg, pause at the top.
- **Regress to:** Reverse Hyper (Bench, Light) (G1); 45 Degree Back Extension (Bodyweight) (G1). **Or regress by:** Superman, bird dog, shorter range.
- **Same level swaps:** Prone Cobra (Chek); Superman (Alternating); 45 Degree Back Extension
- **Cautions:** None specific. Good for most back pain when kept to neutral. Avoid loaded flexion at the bottom for osteoporosis.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8
- **Coach sources:** DeFranco (reverse hyper), McGill, Paul Chek (prone cobra)

## Back Extension (Hold Plate)

`HGB-046 | G2 | Hinge: back extension | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Plate
- **Why we use it:** Strengthens the back extensors and glutes, improving posture and back resilience. Reverse hypers decompress the spine as they train. Extend to neutral only: the goal is a strong, straight spine, not arching.
- **Muscles:** Spinal erectors, glutes, hamstrings
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Hinge at the hips, keep the spine long. 2) Lift to a straight line from head to heels using the glutes. 3) Lower with control.
- **Common faults:** Hyperextending at the top; Swinging/using momentum; Rounding heavily at the bottom under load.
- **Progress to:** Paused DB RDL (G3); Hang Clean Pull (G3); Double KB Swing (G3). **Or progress by:** Hold a plate, single leg, pause at the top.
- **Regress to:** Reverse Hyper (Bench, Light) (G1); 45 Degree Back Extension (Bodyweight) (G1). **Or regress by:** Superman, bird dog, shorter range.
- **Same level swaps:** Prone Cobra (Chek); Reverse Hyper (Bench); Superman (Alternating)
- **Cautions:** None specific. Good for most back pain when kept to neutral. Avoid loaded flexion at the bottom for osteoporosis.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8
- **Coach sources:** DeFranco (reverse hyper), McGill, Paul Chek (prone cobra)

## Barbell Good Morning

`HGB-047 | G3 | Hinge: good morning | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Barbell
- **Why we use it:** Load sits on the upper back while the hips hinge, which strengthens the hamstrings and back extensors. Bodyweight and banded versions are great hinge teaching tools; barbell versions are advanced. ATG style seated good mornings build hamstring and back mobility.
- **This variation:** Barbell: allows the heaviest loading for maximum strength and bone stimulus; earn it with technique (usually G3 to G4, Teams).
- **Muscles:** Hamstrings, glutes, spinal erectors
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Soft knees, brace, push the hips back. 2) Keep the spine long and neutral. 3) Stand up by driving the hips forward.
- **Common faults:** Rounding the spine; Bending the knees too much; Going deeper than hamstring length allows.
- **Progress to:** Rack Pull (G4); Block Pull (G4); Sumo Deadlift (G4). **Or progress by:** Band → light barbell → SSB good morning, tempo, pause.
- **Regress to:** SSB Good Morning (G2); Seated Good Morning (G2); Banded Good Morning (G2). **Or regress by:** Bodyweight, dowel hinge drill.
- **Same level swaps:** Barbell Romanian Deadlift; Paused DB RDL; Double KB Romanian Deadlift
- **Cautions:** Low back. Loaded good mornings are not for low back pain. Keep loads light and range controlled for 40+.
- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9
- **Coach sources:** Westside/DeFranco, Ben Patrick (seated), Poliquin

## Cable Romanian Deadlift

`HGB-048 | G2 | Hinge: Romanian deadlift | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Cable machine
- **Why we use it:** The RDL starts from the top and lowers the weight by pushing the hips back, so it builds hamstrings and glutes in a lengthened position with low skill demand. It's the best hamstring builder for most members and a staple for posture and back resilience.
- **This variation:** Cable: constant tension through the whole range with smooth, joint friendly resistance.
- **Muscles:** Hamstrings, glutes, spinal erectors, grip
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Soft knees, weight close to the legs. 2) Push the hips back, slide the weight down the thighs, keep the back flat. 3) Stop when the hamstrings are tight (usually mid shin), drive the hips forward to stand.
- **Common faults:** Rounding the back to go lower; Squatting it by bending the knees too much; Weight drifting away from the legs.
- **Progress to:** Paused DB RDL (G3); Barbell Romanian Deadlift (G3); Double KB Romanian Deadlift (G3). **Or progress by:** DB → double KB → trap bar → barbell RDL, tempo (4s lowering), pauses, deficit.
- **Regress to:** KB Deadlift (G1); DB Deadlift (G1); Sumo KB Deadlift (G1). **Or regress by:** KB deadlift from blocks, cable pull through, hinge dowel drill, reduce range.
- **Same level swaps:** Tempo DB RDL; Trap Bar RDL; Snatch Grip RDL
- **Cautions:** None specific. Back friendly with good form and controlled range. Reduce range for tight hamstrings or low back sensitivity.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8
- **Coach sources:** Poliquin, Cosgrove, DeFranco

## Seated Good Morning

`HGB-049 | G2 | Hinge: good morning | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Barbell
- **Why we use it:** Load sits on the upper back while the hips hinge, which strengthens the hamstrings and back extensors. Bodyweight and banded versions are great hinge teaching tools; barbell versions are advanced. ATG style seated good mornings build hamstring and back mobility.
- **Muscles:** Hamstrings, glutes, spinal erectors
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Soft knees, brace, push the hips back. 2) Keep the spine long and neutral. 3) Stand up by driving the hips forward.
- **Common faults:** Rounding the spine; Bending the knees too much; Going deeper than hamstring length allows.
- **Progress to:** Barbell Good Morning (G3); Barbell Romanian Deadlift (G3); Paused DB RDL (G3). **Or progress by:** Band → light barbell → SSB good morning, tempo, pause.
- **Regress to:** Bodyweight Good Morning (G1); Hip Hinge to Wall (G1); Hip Hinge Dowel Drill (G1). **Or regress by:** Bodyweight, dowel hinge drill.
- **Same level swaps:** SSB Good Morning; Banded Good Morning; Single Leg Good Morning
- **Cautions:** Low back. Loaded good mornings are not for low back pain. Keep loads light and range controlled for 40+.

## Jefferson Curl (Light)

`HGB-050 | G4 | Hinge: loaded spinal flexion (mobility) | STRONG | Group: No | Impact: none | Teams only: Yes | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Ben Patrick's loaded spinal flexion drill: very light load, rolling down one vertebra at a time to build strength and tolerance in flexion. Used for back resilience and hamstring flexibility in healthy, well trained people.
- **This variation:** Reduced range/load version: used for rehab, beginners, warm ups or flare up days.
- **Muscles:** Spinal erectors and hamstrings in a lengthened position
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Stand on a box with a very light weight. 2) Tuck the chin and roll down slowly, one segment at a time. 3) Roll back up from the bottom, slow and controlled.
- **Common faults:** Going heavy; Rushing; Doing it when the back is irritated.
- **Progress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or progress by:** Tiny load increases only after months.
- **Regress to:** Seated Good Morning (G2); Cat Cow (G1); Toe Touch to Squat (G1). **Or regress by:** Seated good morning (ATG), cat cow, toe touch to squat.
- **Cautions:** Low back, Osteoporosis/osteopenia. CONTRAINDICATED for osteoporosis/osteopenia, disc problems, acute back pain and most beginners. G4 only, Teams, coach approved.
- **Group swap:** Teams only (heavy or high skill): in groups use a G3 regression from the Regress to list
- **Default prescription:** 2 sets x 5 to 8 very slow reps, bodyweight or very light
- **Coach sources:** Ben Patrick (ATG)

## Banded Good Morning

`HGB-051 | G2 | Hinge: good morning | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Barbell, Resistance band (confirm)
- **Why we use it:** Load sits on the upper back while the hips hinge, which strengthens the hamstrings and back extensors. Bodyweight and banded versions are great hinge teaching tools; barbell versions are advanced. ATG style seated good mornings build hamstring and back mobility.
- **This variation:** Band resistance gets harder at the top (accommodating resistance) and can cue better positions such as knees out.
- **Muscles:** Hamstrings, glutes, spinal erectors
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Soft knees, brace, push the hips back. 2) Keep the spine long and neutral. 3) Stand up by driving the hips forward.
- **Common faults:** Rounding the spine; Bending the knees too much; Going deeper than hamstring length allows.
- **Progress to:** Barbell Good Morning (G3); Barbell Romanian Deadlift (G3); Paused DB RDL (G3). **Or progress by:** Band → light barbell → SSB good morning, tempo, pause.
- **Regress to:** Bodyweight Good Morning (G1); Hip Hinge to Wall (G1); Hip Hinge Dowel Drill (G1). **Or regress by:** Bodyweight, dowel hinge drill.
- **Same level swaps:** SSB Good Morning; Seated Good Morning; Single Leg Good Morning
- **Cautions:** Low back. Loaded good mornings are not for low back pain. Keep loads light and range controlled for 40+.
- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9
- **Coach sources:** Westside/DeFranco, Ben Patrick (seated), Poliquin

## Clean Pull (Barbell)

`HGB-052 | G4 | Power: Olympic lift / derivative | HYBRID, STRONG | Group: No | Impact: none | Teams only: Yes | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Barbell
- **Why we use it:** Explosive triple extension (ankles, knees, hips) trains power and rate of force development. Power declines faster than strength with age, so it must be trained, but the skill demand is high. DB, KB and landmine versions are far easier to learn and safer for groups than barbell versions.
- **This variation:** Barbell: allows the heaviest loading for maximum strength and bone stimulus; earn it with technique (usually G3 to G4, Teams).
- **Muscles:** Whole body: glutes, quads, hamstrings, traps, shoulders
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Start in a strong hinge with the weight close. 2) Explode up through the legs and hips, shrug and pull the elbows high. 3) Catch softly in a strong rack position (or overhead), stand tall.
- **Common faults:** Pulling early with the arms; Weight swinging away from the body; Catching with the back arched.
- **Progress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or progress by:** Pull → hang version → from the floor; DB → KB → barbell.
- **Regress to:** Power Clean (G3); Hang Clean Pull (G3); Hang Power Clean (G3). **Or regress by:** Pull only (no catch), KB swing, med ball scoop toss, landmine clean.
- **Same level swaps:** Barbell Push Jerk; Double KB Clean; KB High Pull (Single Arm)
- **Cautions:** Low back, Osteoporosis/osteopenia, Shoulder. Wrists, shoulders and low back need to be healthy. Barbell versions: Teams G4 only. Not for osteoporosis without careful progression.
- **Group swap:** Teams only (heavy or high skill): in groups use a G3 regression from the Regress to list
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 5 sets x 3 to 6 reps, full recovery (60 to 120s), stop when speed drops
- **Coach sources:** DeFranco, Cosgrove (power block), Gambetta

## Cable Pull Through

`HGB-053 | G1 | Hinge: hip extension accessory | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Cable machine
- **Why we use it:** Cable/band pull throughs teach the hip hinge with the load pulling from behind, so people naturally sit the hips back and finish with the glutes. Kickbacks and quadruped hip extensions isolate the glutes for activation and rehab.
- **This variation:** Cable: constant tension through the whole range with smooth, joint friendly resistance.
- **Muscles:** Glutes, hamstrings
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Face away from the cable, rope between the legs. 2) Hinge back letting the rope pull the hips back. 3) Drive the hips through and squeeze the glutes, stand tall.
- **Common faults:** Pulling with the arms; Squatting instead of hinging; Leaning back at the top.
- **Progress to:** Single Arm Cable Pull Through (G2); KB Swings (G2); KB Swing (Power) (G2). **Or progress by:** Heavier, pause at the top, progress to KB swing.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Band version, shorter range.
- **Same level swaps:** Cable Kickback; Band Pull Through; Cable Pull Through (Light)
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very back friendly. A great swing and deadlift regression.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8
- **Coach sources:** Cosgrove, McGill, Boyle

## Hang Clean Pull

- **Why we use it:** Explosive triple extension (ankles, knees, hips) trains power and rate of force development. - **Regress to:** Snatch Grip RDL (G2); Barbell Hip Thrust (G2); Seated Good Morning (G2). **Or regress by:** Pull only (no catch), KB swing, med ball scoop toss, landmine clean.
- **Same level swaps:** Hang Power Clean; Hang Power Snatch; Power Clean
- **Cautions:** Low back, Osteoporosis/osteopenia, Shoulder. Wrists, shoulders and low back need to be healthy. Barbell versions: Teams G4 only. Not for osteoporosis without careful progression.

## Band Pull Through

## Snatch Grip Deadlift

`HGB-056 | G4 | Hinge: barbell deadlift | STRONG | Group: No | Impact: none | Teams only: Yes | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Barbell
- **Why we use it:** The heaviest total body strength lift. Builds posterior chain strength, grip and bone density (LIFTMOR). Block and rack pulls shorten the range for beginners or back sensitivity; deficit and paused versions are advanced.
- **Muscles:** Glutes, hamstrings, back, grip, whole body
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Bar over the middle of the foot, shins close. 2) Grip, chest up, pull the slack out, brace hard. 3) Push the floor away, bar stays close, lock out with the glutes.
- **Common faults:** Rounding the back; Bar drifting away from the legs; Hyperextending at the top.
- **Progress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or progress by:** Add load, pause off the floor, deficit, rep max progressions.
- **Regress to:** Barbell Romanian Deadlift (G3); Paused DB RDL (G3); Trap Bar Deadlift (G3). **Or regress by:** Block/rack pull, trap bar deadlift, KB deadlift.
- **Same level swaps:** Rack Pull; Block Pull; Sumo Deadlift
- **Cautions:** Low back, Pelvic floor. Highest low back demand. Not for active back pain. Trap bar is the default for most 40+ members. Teams G4 only for straight bar.
- **Group swap:** Teams only (heavy or high skill): in groups use a G3 regression from the Regress to list
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8
- **Coach sources:** DeFranco, LIFTMOR research, Poliquin

## Landmine Romanian Deadlift

`HGB-057 | G2 | Hinge: Romanian deadlift | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Landmine (confirm)
- **Why we use it:** The RDL starts from the top and lowers the weight by pushing the hips back, so it builds hamstrings and glutes in a lengthened position with low skill demand. It's the best hamstring builder for most members and a staple for posture and back resilience.
- **This variation:** Landmine: the arc path is shoulder and back friendly and very easy to learn.
- **Muscles:** Hamstrings, glutes, spinal erectors, grip
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Soft knees, weight close to the legs. 2) Push the hips back, slide the weight down the thighs, keep the back flat. 3) Stop when the hamstrings are tight (usually mid shin), drive the hips forward to stand.
- **Common faults:** Rounding the back to go lower; Squatting it by bending the knees too much; Weight drifting away from the legs.
- **Progress to:** Paused DB RDL (G3); Barbell Romanian Deadlift (G3); Double KB Romanian Deadlift (G3). **Or progress by:** DB → double KB → trap bar → barbell RDL, tempo (4s lowering), pauses, deficit.
- **Regress to:** Landmine Deadlift (G1); KB Deadlift (G1); DB Deadlift (G1). **Or regress by:** KB deadlift from blocks, cable pull through, hinge dowel drill, reduce range.
- **Same level swaps:** Tempo DB RDL; Trap Bar RDL; Snatch Grip RDL
- **Cautions:** None specific. Back friendly with good form and controlled range. Reduce range for tight hamstrings or low back sensitivity.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8
- **Coach sources:** Poliquin, Cosgrove, DeFranco

## Dead Bug Bridge Hold

`HGB-058 | G1 | Core: anti extension (dead bug) | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Keeps the low back flat while the arms and legs move: anti extension control and coordination. Safe for almost everyone and the foundation of bracing (McGill, Chek).
- **This variation:** Isometric: builds strength and tendon tolerance in a fixed position with minimal joint irritation.
- **Muscles:** Deep abs, hip flexors, coordination
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Back flat, ribs down, knees and arms up. 2) Slowly extend the opposite arm and leg while breathing out. 3) Return and swap without the back arching.
- **Common faults:** Low back lifting; Moving fast; Holding the breath.
- **Progress to:** Plank Saw (G2); RKC Plank (G2); Front Plank (G2). **Or progress by:** Straighter legs, band resisted, KB pullover, slower.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Heel taps, arms only.
- **Same level swaps:** Dead Bug; Dead Bug Heel Taps; Dead Bug (Wall Press)
- **Cautions:** None specific. Back pain friendly. Pelvic floor friendly.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 6 to 10 reps each side (or 20 to 40s), slow and controlled
- **Coach sources:** McGill, Paul Chek, Boyle

## Landmine Deadlift

`HGB-059 | G1 | Hinge: deadlift (KB/DB/landmine) | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Landmine (confirm)
- **Why we use it:** The safest way to teach lifting from the floor. Picking things up is a life skill (Primal Pattern 'bend'). Raising the bell on blocks reduces range for beginners and back pain; suitcase versions add anti lateral flexion.
- **This variation:** Landmine: the arc path is shoulder and back friendly and very easy to learn.
- **Muscles:** Glutes, hamstrings, back, grip
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Bell between the feet (or beside for suitcase), hinge down with a flat back. 2) Grip, pull the shoulders down, brace. 3) Push the floor away and stand tall, squeeze the glutes.
- **Common faults:** Squatting down too low; Rounding to reach the bell; Leaning back at the top.
- **Progress to:** Landmine Romanian Deadlift (G2); KB Swings (G2); Tempo DB RDL (G2). **Or progress by:** Heavier bell, double KB, lower to the floor, progress to RDL, swing and trap bar.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Bell on a block/step, hinge drill.
- **Same level swaps:** KB Deadlift; DB Deadlift; Sumo KB Deadlift
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very back friendly. Elevate the bell on a step for limited hip mobility or back history.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8
- **Coach sources:** Dan John, McGill, Cosgrove

## Double KB Swing

`HGB-060 | G3 | Hinge: ballistic (power) | BURN, HYBRID, STRONG | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Kettlebell
- **Why we use it:** The king of hinge conditioning (Dan John, Pavel). Trains explosive hip extension (power) and heart rate at the same time with no impact on the knees. Excellent for fat loss, posture and glute strength. Dead stop versions teach control; single arm versions add anti rotation.
- **This variation:** Double KB: heavier total load plus a front rack or bilateral grip demand.
- **Muscles:** Glutes, hamstrings, core, grip, cardiovascular system
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Hike the bell back high between the thighs. 2) Snap the hips forward, squeeze the glutes, let the bell float to chest height. 3) Let it fall, hinge late, keep the spine neutral.
- **Common faults:** Squatting the swing instead of hinging; Lifting with the arms; Leaning back at the top.
- **Progress to:** Double KB Clean (G4); KB High Pull (Single Arm) (G4); Barbell Push Jerk (G4). **Or progress by:** Heavier bell, single arm, alternating, swings EMOM, heavier with fewer reps for power.
- **Regress to:** KB Swings (G2); KB Swing (Power) (G2); American KB Swing (G2). **Or regress by:** KB deadlift, dead stop swing, lighter bell, cable pull through.
- **Same level swaps:** Single Arm KB Swing; Single Arm KB Swing to Catch; Single Arm KB Swing (Anti Rotation)
- **Cautions:** Low back. Back friendly when the hinge is good. Teach the KB deadlift first. Not for acute low back pain. American (overhead) swings stress shoulders and low back: use hip height swings instead.
- **Default prescription:** 4 to 10 sets x 10 to 20 reps, or EMOM; 'hike, snap, float'
- **Coach sources:** Dan John, Pavel Tsatsouline, Cosgrove

# 04. HINGE PATTERN: UNILATERAL

*Hip dominant, single leg and staggered stance*

**Grade ladder at a glance** (use this to slot every member into the same session at their level):

- **G1**: Cable Kickback, Banded Glute Kickback, Quadruped Hip Extension, Quadruped Hip Extension (Ankle Weight), Single Leg Bench Hamstring Bridge, Kickstand Hip Thrust, Single Leg Landmine Hip Thrust, Standing Cable Hip Extension
- **G2**: Single Leg RDL (Bodyweight), Alternating KB Swing, Supported Single Leg RDL, Kickstand RDL (DB), Single Arm Cable Pull Through, Kickstand RDL (KB), Long Lever Single Leg Bridge, Reverse Lunge to RDL, Single Leg Good Morning, Airplane (Hip Rotation Single Leg Hinge), B Stance KB Deadlift, Banded Airplane, Staggered Stance Trap Bar Deadlift, Single Leg Glute Bridge, Single Leg Glute Bridge Hold, Single Leg Hip Thrust, Frog Stance Single Leg Bridge, Single Leg Hip Thrust (DB), Single Leg Hip Thrust (Barbell), Lateral Lunge to RDL, Shoulder Elevated Single Leg Bridge March, Single Leg Glute Bridge (Mini Band), Single Leg Bridge off Bench, Split Stance Cable RDL, Single Leg Hinge to Overhead Reach
- **G3**: Single Arm KB Swing to Catch, Kickstand RDL (Barbell), Single Leg RDL (DB), Single Leg RDL (KB), Contralateral Single Leg RDL, Ipsilateral Single Leg RDL, Single Leg RDL (Double KB), Bulgarian Split Squat (Forward Lean), Landmine Single Leg RDL, Cable Single Leg RDL, Step Up to Single Leg RDL, Single Leg RDL to Row, Single Leg RDL to Knee Drive, TRX Single Leg RDL, Single Leg RDL with Reach, Single Leg RDL Iso Hold, Single Leg Deadlift to Box, Single Leg Deadlift (Trap Bar), Single Leg Hip Thrust (Paused), Curtsy to Single Leg RDL, Single Leg Swiss Ball Curl, Single Leg TRX Hamstring Curl, Single Leg RDL to Press, Single Leg Back Extension, Single Arm KB Swing
- **G4**: Offset KB Single Leg RDL, Single Leg Slider Curl

✱ = not for group sessions (impact).

## Single Leg RDL (Bodyweight)

`HGU-001 | G2 | Hinge: single leg / staggered | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Single leg hinges build hamstring and glute strength, balance and hip stability one side at a time, and they spare the spine because loads are lighter. Kickstand and B stance versions give a stepping stone with the back foot for support. Hip airplanes train hip rotation control (great for golf).
- **Muscles:** Hamstrings, glutes (incl. glute med), foot and ankle stability
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Stand on one leg with a soft knee, other leg reaching back. 2) Hinge forward as one straight line from head to heel, hips square. 3) Drive the standing heel into the floor and squeeze the glute to stand.
- **Common faults:** Hips opening up (rotating) towards the ceiling; Rounding the back to reach the floor; Standing knee locked straight.
- **Progress to:** TRX Single Leg RDL (G3); Single Leg RDL (DB) (G3); Single Leg RDL (KB) (G3). **Or progress by:** Kickstand → full single leg, add load (DB/KB, double KB, landmine), slower tempo, add a row or reach.
- **Regress to:** KB Deadlift (G1); DB Deadlift (G1); Sumo KB Deadlift (G1). **Or regress by:** Supported single leg RDL (hand on rig), kickstand RDL, bodyweight.
- **Same level swaps:** Kickstand RDL; Banded Airplane; Kickstand RDL (DB)
- **Cautions:** None specific. Back friendly. Balance limits load: use a support or kickstand first. Excellent for golfers and runners.
- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9 (each leg)
- **Coach sources:** Boyle, Cosgrove, Gambetta

## Alternating KB Swing

- **Common faults:** Squatting the swing instead of hinging; Lifting with the arms; Leaning back at the top.
- **Progress to:** Double KB Swing (G3); Single Arm KB Swing (G3); Single Arm KB Swing to Catch (G3). **Or progress by:** Heavier bell, single arm, alternating, swings EMOM, heavier with fewer reps for power.
- **Regress to:** KB Deadlift (G1); Sumo KB Deadlift (G1); Elevated KB Deadlift (G1). **Or regress by:** KB deadlift, dead stop swing, lighter bell, cable pull through.
- **Same level swaps:** KB Swings; KB Swing (Power); American KB Swing
- **Cautions:** Low back. Back friendly when the hinge is good. Teach the KB deadlift first. Not for acute low back pain. American (overhead) swings stress shoulders and low back: use hip height swings instead.
- **Default prescription:** 4 to 10 sets x 10 to 20 reps, or EMOM; 'hike, snap, float'
- **Coach sources:** Dan John, Pavel Tsatsouline, Cosgrove

## Single Arm KB Swing to Catch

`HGU-004 | G3 | Hinge: ballistic (power) | BURN, HYBRID, STRONG | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Kettlebell
- **Why we use it:** The king of hinge conditioning (Dan John, Pavel). Trains explosive hip extension (power) and heart rate at the same time with no impact on the knees. Excellent for fat loss, posture and glute strength. Dead stop versions teach control; single arm versions add anti rotation.
- **This variation:** One sided loading adds an anti rotation / anti lateral flexion core challenge and exposes left/right differences.
- **Muscles:** Glutes, hamstrings, core, grip, cardiovascular system
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Hike the bell back high between the thighs. 2) Snap the hips forward, squeeze the glutes, let the bell float to chest height. 3) Let it fall, hinge late, keep the spine neutral.
- **Common faults:** Squatting the swing instead of hinging; Lifting with the arms; Leaning back at the top.
- **Progress to:** Double KB Clean (G4); KB High Pull (Single Arm) (G4); Barbell Push Jerk (G4). **Or progress by:** Heavier bell, single arm, alternating, swings EMOM, heavier with fewer reps for power.
- **Regress to:** KB Swings (G2); KB Swing (Power) (G2); American KB Swing (G2). **Or regress by:** KB deadlift, dead stop swing, lighter bell, cable pull through.
- **Same level swaps:** Double KB Swing; Single Arm KB Swing; Single Arm KB Swing (Anti Rotation)
- **Cautions:** Low back. Back friendly when the hinge is good. Teach the KB deadlift first. Not for acute low back pain. American (overhead) swings stress shoulders and low back: use hip height swings instead.
- **Default prescription:** 4 to 10 sets x 10 to 20 reps, or EMOM; 'hike, snap, float'
- **Coach sources:** Dan John, Pavel Tsatsouline, Cosgrove

## Single Arm Cable Pull Through

`HGU-006 | G2 | Hinge: hip extension accessory | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Cable machine
- **Why we use it:** Cable/band pull throughs teach the hip hinge with the load pulling from behind, so people naturally sit the hips back and finish with the glutes. Kickbacks and quadruped hip extensions isolate the glutes for activation and rehab.
- **This variation:** One sided loading adds an anti rotation / anti lateral flexion core challenge and exposes left/right differences. Cable: constant tension through the whole range with smooth, joint friendly resistance.
- **Muscles:** Glutes, hamstrings
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Face away from the cable, rope between the legs. 2) Hinge back letting the rope pull the hips back. 3) Drive the hips through and squeeze the glutes, stand tall.
- **Common faults:** Pulling with the arms; Squatting instead of hinging; Leaning back at the top.
- **Progress to:** Double KB Swing (G3); Single Arm KB Swing (G3); Single Arm KB Swing to Catch (G3). **Or progress by:** Heavier, pause at the top, progress to KB swing.
- **Regress to:** Cable Kickback (G1); Band Pull Through (G1); Cable Pull Through (G1). **Or regress by:** Band version, shorter range.
- **Same level swaps:** KB Swings; KB Swing (Power); American KB Swing
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very back friendly. A great swing and deadlift regression.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8
- **Coach sources:** Cosgrove, McGill, Boyle

## Single Leg Bench Hamstring Bridge

`HGU-016 | G1 | Hinge: hip extension (bridge / thrust) | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Box / bench / step
- **Why we use it:** Bridges and hip thrusts train the glutes at their strongest point (full hip extension) with almost no spinal load. They are essential for back pain, knee pain, posture, sprinting and golf power, and are safe for nearly everyone. Single leg versions fix imbalances.
- **Muscles:** Glutes, hamstrings
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Feet flat, shins vertical at the top. 2) Tuck the ribs down, drive through the heels and squeeze the glutes to lift. 3) Pause at the top without arching the low back, lower slowly.
- **Common faults:** Arching the low back instead of extending the hips; Feet too far away (all hamstrings); Pushing through the toes.
- **Progress to:** Paused Hip Thrust (G2); Barbell Hip Thrust (G2); Hip Thrust (Paused) (G2). **Or progress by:** Bridge → hip thrust off a bench → load (DB, barbell) → single leg, add pauses or bands.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Floor bridge, shorter range, isometric hold.
- **Same level swaps:** Frog Pump; Glute Bridge; Hip Thrust (DB)
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very joint friendly. Use a pad on the hips when loaded. Shoulder elevated versions need a stable bench.
- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9 (pause 1 to 2s at the top)
- **Coach sources:** Cosgrove, McGill, Boyle
