- **Muscles:** Shoulders, core, cardio

- **Common faults:** Locking elbows; Arms only; Dropping the guard.
- **Progress to:** Crab Walk (G2); KB Swings (G2); Bear Crawl (G2). **Or progress by:** Faster, light DBs (no lockout).

## KB Complex

`CON-038 | G2 | Conditioning: protocol / format | BURN, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Kettlebell
- **Why we use it:** Session formats rather than single exercises. Complexes (Cosgrove) chain lifts without putting the weight down; EMOMs, AMRAPs and ladders control density and keep groups together. Build them only from exercises the group can perform safely while tired.
- **Muscles:** Depends on the exercises chosen
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Pick 3 to 6 exercises the members already own. 2) Set the work:rest and level targets (G1 to G4). 3) Keep quality high, cap volume.
- **Common faults:** Choosing technical lifts for high fatigue formats; No level options; Too long.
- **Progress to:** KB Snatch (G3); KB Clean and Press (G3); DB Thrusters (G3). **Or progress by:** More rounds, heavier, less rest.
- **Regress to:** Farmer's Carry Shuttle (G1); Sled Push (G1); Sled Pull (G1). **Or regress by:** Fewer rounds, lighter, more rest.
- **Same level swaps:** DB Complex; EMOM (Mixed); AMRAP Circuit
- **Cautions:** None specific. Exclude jumping in group formats. Avoid heavy spinal loading late in fatigue.
- **Default prescription:** 8 to 20 min blocks
- **Coach sources:** Cosgrove (complexes, density), Dan John

## Partner Rower Relay

`CON-039 | G1 | Conditioning: erg / walking | BURN, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Rower
- **Why we use it:** The bike, rower and ski erg give big conditioning with no impact, and every level can work at their own intensity. Zone 2 builds the aerobic base (Attia); short sprints suit menopause and fat loss (Sims, Cosgrove hierarchy). Backward walking (treadmill or sled) is Ben Patrick's knee warm up.
- **Muscles:** Heart and lungs, legs (bike/rower), upper body (ski/rower)
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Bike: push and pull with arms and legs, steady cadence. 2) Rower: legs, body, arms; then arms, body, legs. 3) Ski: hinge and pull down, drive the hips.
- **Common faults:** Rowing with the arms first; Hunched posture; Going out too hard in intervals.
- **Progress to:** Crab Walk (G2); KB Swings (G2); Bear Crawl (G2). **Or progress by:** Longer work, shorter rest, higher watts/calories, more rounds.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Easier pace, shorter intervals, more rest.
- **Same level swaps:** Rower 500m; Rower Intervals; Rower Steady State
- **Cautions:** None specific. Low impact. Rower and ski: watch low back flexion. Treadmill sprints involve impact.
- **Default prescription:** Intervals: e.g. 6 to 10 x 15 to 30s hard / 60 to 90s easy, or 20 to 40 min steady (zone 2)
- **Coach sources:** Attia (zone 2, VO2), Cosgrove (intervals), Stacy Sims (sprints), Ben Patrick (backward walking)

- **Progress to:** DB Thrusters (G3); KB Snatch (G3); Barbell Complex (G3). **Or progress by:** More rounds, heavier, less rest.
- **Regress to:** Farmer's Carry Shuttle (G1); Sled Push (G1); Sled Pull (G1). **Or regress by:** Fewer rounds, lighter, more rest.
- **Same level swaps:** KB Complex; EMOM (Mixed); AMRAP Circuit
- **Cautions:** None specific. Exclude jumping in group formats. Avoid heavy spinal loading late in fatigue.

- **Coach sources:** Cosgrove (complexes, density), Dan John

## DB Thrusters

`CON-046 | G3 | Squat + vertical push (combination) | BURN, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Dumbbells (confirm)
- **Why we use it:** Links a squat and an overhead press into one total body movement. Very metabolic, great for BURN and HYBRID sessions, and the legs help drive the weight overhead so people can press more.
- **Muscles:** Quads, glutes, shoulders, triceps, core
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Squat with the weight in the rack. 2) Drive up hard and use that momentum to press overhead. 3) Lock out with biceps by the ears, ribs down, then lower back to the rack.
- **Common faults:** Pressing before the legs finish the drive; Arching the low back at the top; Losing the rack position and squatting with the elbows dropped.
- **Progress to:** Barbell Thruster (G4); Double KB Front Squat to Press (G4); Barbell Front Rack Squat to Press (G4). **Or progress by:** Add load, double KBs, barbell, more rounds or density.
- **Regress to:** DB Complex (G2); Crab Walk (G2); KB Swings (G2). **Or regress by:** Goblet squat to press, landmine squat to press, split into separate squat and press.
- **Same level swaps:** DB Thruster; DB Squat to Overhead Press; KB Thruster
- **Cautions:** Shoulder. Needs pain free overhead range. With shoulder pain swap to squat to landmine press. Watch technique as fatigue builds in circuits.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 8 to 12 reps, or 30 to 40s in circuits
- **Coach sources:** Cosgrove (MRT), DeFranco

## Tabata Bike

`CON-047 | G1 | Conditioning: erg / walking | BURN, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Assault bike / bike
- **Why we use it:** The bike, rower and ski erg give big conditioning with no impact, and every level can work at their own intensity. Zone 2 builds the aerobic base (Attia); short sprints suit menopause and fat loss (Sims, Cosgrove hierarchy). Backward walking (treadmill or sled) is Ben Patrick's knee warm up.
- **Muscles:** Heart and lungs, legs (bike/rower), upper body (ski/rower)
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Bike: push and pull with arms and legs, steady cadence. 2) Rower: legs, body, arms; then arms, body, legs. 3) Ski: hinge and pull down, drive the hips.
- **Common faults:** Rowing with the arms first; Hunched posture; Going out too hard in intervals.
- **Progress to:** Crab Walk (G2); KB Swings (G2); Bear Crawl (G2). **Or progress by:** Longer work, shorter rest, higher watts/calories, more rounds.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Easier pace, shorter intervals, more rest.
- **Same level swaps:** Bike (Easy); Bike Erg Intervals; Assault Bike Sprint
- **Cautions:** None specific. Low impact. Rower and ski: watch low back flexion. Treadmill sprints involve impact.
- **Default prescription:** Intervals: e.g. 6 to 10 x 15 to 30s hard / 60 to 90s easy, or 20 to 40 min steady (zone 2)
- **Coach sources:** Attia (zone 2, VO2), Cosgrove (intervals), Stacy Sims (sprints), Ben Patrick (backward walking)

## Sled Push and Bike Couplet

`CON-051 | G1 | Carry / gait: sled push, pull and drag | BURN, HYBRID, STRONG | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Sled, Assault bike / bike
- **Why we use it:** The sled is the most joint friendly strength and conditioning tool in the gym: concentric only, so almost no soreness, no impact and no technique to fail. Ben Patrick uses backward drags for knee health; DeFranco uses pushes for conditioning. Every member at every level can use it.
- **Muscles:** Quads, glutes, calves, whole body conditioning
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Push: arms extended or bent, body at 45 degrees, drive through the balls of the feet. 2) Drag backward: lean back, small steps, push through the front of the foot (knees over toes). 3) Keep steady steps and a neutral spine.
- **Common faults:** Hips too high or too low; Rounding the back; Taking huge steps that slow the sled.
- **Progress to:** Prowler Push (G3); Sled Sprint (Push) (G3); Sled Sprint (Pull) (G3). **Or progress by:** More weight, faster (sprints), longer distance, less rest.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Lighter, slower, shorter distance.
- **Same level swaps:** Sled Push; Sled Pull; Sled Row (Rope)
- **Cautions:** None specific. Almost universally safe. Backward drag is a knee pain staple. Heavy pushes raise blood pressure: keep breathing.
- **Default prescription:** 6 to 10 x 15 to 25m, walk back recovery; or 3 to 5 min backward drag in warm up
- **Coach sources:** Ben Patrick (ATG), DeFranco, Boyle

## Every Minute Carry and Swing

`CON-053 | G2 | Hinge: ballistic (power) | BURN, HYBRID, STRONG | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Kettlebell
- **Why we use it:** The king of hinge conditioning (Dan John, Pavel). Trains explosive hip extension (power) and heart rate at the same time with no impact on the knees. Excellent for fat loss, posture and glute strength. Dead stop versions teach control; single arm versions add anti rotation.
- **Muscles:** Glutes, hamstrings, core, grip, cardiovascular system
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Hike the bell back high between the thighs. 2) Snap the hips forward, squeeze the glutes, let the bell float to chest height. 3) Let it fall, hinge late, keep the spine neutral.
- **Common faults:** Squatting the swing instead of hinging; Lifting with the arms; Leaning back at the top.
- **Progress to:** Double KB Swing (G3); Single Arm KB Swing (G3); Single Arm KB Swing to Catch (G3). **Or progress by:** Heavier bell, single arm, alternating, swings EMOM, heavier with fewer reps for power.
- **Regress to:** KB Deadlift (G1); Sumo KB Deadlift (G1); Elevated KB Deadlift (G1). **Or regress by:** KB deadlift, dead stop swing, lighter bell, cable pull through.
- **Same level swaps:** KB Swings; KB Swing (Power); American KB Swing
- **Cautions:** Low back. Back friendly when the hinge is good. Teach the KB deadlift first. Not for acute low back pain. American (overhead) swings stress shoulders and low back: use hip height swings instead.
- **Default prescription:** 4 to 10 sets x 10 to 20 reps, or EMOM; 'hike, snap, float'
- **Coach sources:** Dan John, Pavel Tsatsouline, Cosgrove

# 15. REHAB: SHOULDER

*Rotator cuff, scapula, mobility and stability*

**Grade ladder at a glance** (use this to slot every member into the same session at their level):

- **G1**: Pendulum Swings, Serratus Wall Slide (Foam Roller), Table Slides, Serratus Punch (Band), Wall Slides, Serratus Punch (DB Supine), Wall Angels, Press Up Plus, Floor Angels, Bear Plank Protraction, Shoulder Flexion with Dowel, Dowel Pass Through, Sleeper Stretch, Turkish Get Up (Light), Doorway Pec Stretch, Isometric External Rotation, Isometric Internal Rotation, Landmine Press (Light), Isometric Shoulder Abduction, Scaption Raise, Side Lying External Rotation (DB), Lu Raise, Band External Rotation, Shrug to Retraction, Band Internal Rotation, Lower Trap Raise (Prone), Cable External Rotation, Wall Ball Circles, Cable Internal Rotation, Body Blade (Band Oscillation), 90/90 External Rotation (Band), Rhythmic Stabilisation (Partner), External Rotation at 90 Degrees (Cable), Quadruped Weight Shift, Prone Y Raise, Band Dislocates, Prone T Raise, Thoracic Extension on Foam Roller, Prone W Raise, Thread the Needle, Prone I Raise, Open Book Stretch, Band Pull Apart, Lat Stretch (Bench), Band Face Pull, Face Pull with External Rotation, Shoulder CARs, Scapula Push Up, Scapula Pull Up, Lat Pulldown (Light, Full Range), Scapula Retraction (TRX), Waiter's Carry (Light)
- **G2**: Bottoms Up KB Hold, Cross Body Stretch, Arm Bar (KB), Half Kneeling Landmine Press, Cable Y Pull, Hanging (Supported)
- **G3**: Bottoms Up KB Carry, Bottoms Up KB Press

✱ = not for group sessions (impact).

## Pendulum Swings

`RSH-001 | G1 | Shoulder mobility: gentle range | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Kettlebell
- **Why we use it:** Gentle shoulder range of motion work. Pendulums and table slides are first stage rehab for stiff or painful shoulders; dowel and band pass throughs maintain overhead and behind body mobility (DeFranco Simple 6).
- **Muscles:** Shoulder joint, capsule, lats, pecs
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Relaxed, no forcing. 2) Move slowly through comfortable range. 3) Breathe.
- **Common faults:** Forcing painful range; Shrugging; Arching to fake range.
- **Progress to:** Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2); Cross Body Stretch (G2). **Or progress by:** Bigger range, narrower grip on pass throughs.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Smaller range, table slides.
- **Same level swaps:** Table Slides; Band Dislocates; Dowel Pass Through
- **Cautions:** None specific. Use pain free range only. Frozen shoulder: refer and follow the physio.
- **Default prescription:** 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down
- **Coach sources:** Squat University, DeFranco (Simple 6), Rehab practice

## Serratus Wall Slide (Foam Roller)

`RSH-002 | G1 | Shoulder: serratus anterior | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Foam roller (confirm)
- **Why we use it:** The serratus holds the shoulder blade against the ribcage and rotates it upward for overhead reaching. Weak serratus = winging and shoulder pain.
- **Muscles:** Serratus anterior
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Arms straight. 2) Push the floor or weight away, spreading the shoulder blades. 3) Return slowly.
- **Common faults:** Bending the elbows; Shrugging; Sagging hips (push up plus).
- **Progress to:** Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2). **Or progress by:** Push up plus, band punch, heavier.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Wall version.
- **Same level swaps:** Press Up Plus; Scapula Push Up; Serratus Punch (Band)
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very shoulder friendly.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8
- **Coach sources:** Cressey, Squat University

## Wall Slides

`RSH-005 | G1 | Shoulder: scapular control (wall slides) | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Sliding the arms up the wall trains the shoulder blade to rotate upward properly, which is key for pain free overhead movement. Part of the Simple 6 style warm up.
- **Muscles:** Lower traps, serratus, T spine extension
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Back or forearms against the wall, ribs down. 2) Slide the arms up keeping contact, shoulders down. 3) Slide back down, squeezing the shoulder blades.
- **Common faults:** Arching the low back; Shrugging; Forcing range.
- **Progress to:** Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2). **Or progress by:** Add a band or lift off at the top.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Smaller range, floor angels.
- **Same level swaps:** Wall Slide; Wall Angels; Floor Angels
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very shoulder friendly.
- **Default prescription:** 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down
- **Coach sources:** Cressey, DeFranco (Simple 6), Squat University

- **Coach sources:** Cressey, Squat University

## Wall Angels

`RSH-007 | G1 | Shoulder: scapular control (wall slides) | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Sliding the arms up the wall trains the shoulder blade to rotate upward properly, which is key for pain free overhead movement. Part of the Simple 6 style warm up.
- **Muscles:** Lower traps, serratus, T spine extension
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Back or forearms against the wall, ribs down. 2) Slide the arms up keeping contact, shoulders down. 3) Slide back down, squeezing the shoulder blades.
- **Common faults:** Arching the low back; Shrugging; Forcing range.
- **Progress to:** Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2). **Or progress by:** Add a band or lift off at the top.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Smaller range, floor angels.
- **Same level swaps:** Wall Slide; Wall Slides; Floor Angels
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very shoulder friendly.
- **Default prescription:** 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down
- **Coach sources:** Cressey, DeFranco (Simple 6), Squat University
- **Also listed in:** Mobility And Warm Up

**Press Up Plus** (G1): full entry under Horizontal Push, ID HPU-035.

## Bear Plank Protraction

`RSH-009 | G1 | Shoulder: serratus anterior | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** The serratus holds the shoulder blade against the ribcage and rotates it upward for overhead reaching. Weak serratus = winging and shoulder pain.
- **Muscles:** Serratus anterior
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Arms straight. 2) Push the floor or weight away, spreading the shoulder blades. 3) Return slowly.
- **Common faults:** Bending the elbows; Shrugging; Sagging hips (push up plus).
- **Progress to:** Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2). **Or progress by:** Push up plus, band punch, heavier.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Wall version.
- **Same level swaps:** Press Up Plus; Scapula Push Up; Serratus Punch (Band)
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very shoulder friendly.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8
- **Coach sources:** Cressey, Squat University

## Shoulder Flexion with Dowel

`RSH-010 | G1 | Shoulder mobility: gentle range | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Dowel (confirm)
- **Why we use it:** Gentle shoulder range of motion work. Pendulums and table slides are first stage rehab for stiff or painful shoulders; dowel and band pass throughs maintain overhead and behind body mobility (DeFranco Simple 6).
- **Muscles:** Shoulder joint, capsule, lats, pecs
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Relaxed, no forcing. 2) Move slowly through comfortable range. 3) Breathe.
- **Common faults:** Forcing painful range; Shrugging; Arching to fake range.
- **Progress to:** Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2). **Or progress by:** Bigger range, narrower grip on pass throughs.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Smaller range, table slides.
- **Same level swaps:** Dowel Pass Through; Table Slides; Pendulum Swings
- **Cautions:** None specific. Use pain free range only. Frozen shoulder: refer and follow the physio.
- **Default prescription:** 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down
- **Coach sources:** Squat University, DeFranco (Simple 6), Rehab practice

**Bottoms Up KB Hold** (G2): full entry under Loaded Carries, ID CAR-041.

## Sleeper Stretch

`RSH-012 | G1 | Mobility: stretch / spinal mobility | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Static and gentle mobility work restores range lost from sitting and ageing. Best used where a screen shows a restriction (Squat University: screen, correct, retest), and to cool down. McKenzie press ups and extension work often relieve disc type back pain; flexion stretches often suit stenosis type pain: individualise.
- **Muscles:** Target muscles and joints vary (named in the exercise)
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Get into position slowly. 2) Breathe out to relax into range, no bouncing. 3) Hold 30 to 60s or do slow reps.
- **Common faults:** Forcing painful range; Holding the breath; Stretching instead of strengthening when stability is the issue.
- **Progress to:** Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2). **Or progress by:** Longer holds, deeper range, add loaded stretching.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Smaller range, supported versions.
- **Same level swaps:** Frog Stretch; Couch Stretch; Elephant Walk
- **Cautions:** None specific. Gentle and safe. Stop if symptoms travel down the leg. Osteoporosis: avoid loaded flexion stretches.
- **Default prescription:** 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down
- **Coach sources:** Squat University, DeFranco (Limber 11), Ben Patrick (couch stretch), McGill

**Bottoms Up KB Press** (G3): full entry under Vertical Push, ID VPU-034.

## Cross Body Stretch

`RSH-013 | G2 | Carry: suitcase / offset | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Dumbbells (confirm), Kettlebell
- **Why we use it:** One side loading turns a carry into an anti lateral flexion core exercise: you must stop the body leaning. McGill calls the suitcase carry one of the best core exercises.
- **Muscles:** Obliques, QL, grip, glute med
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Weight in one hand, stand tall, shoulders level. 2) Walk slowly without leaning towards or away from the weight. 3) Swap hands.
- **Common faults:** Leaning; Shrugging the loaded side; Rushing.
- **Progress to:** Uneven Front Rack Carry (G3); Bottoms Up KB Press (G3); Bottoms Up KB Carry (G3). **Or progress by:** Heavier, march with high knees, longer.
- **Regress to:** Farmer's Carry (G1); Farmer's Carry March (G1); Farmer's Hold (Static) (G1). **Or regress by:** Lighter, static hold.
- **Same level swaps:** Suitcase Hold; Suitcase March; Suitcase Carry
- **Cautions:** None specific. Back pain friendly.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 5 x 20 to 40m (or 30 to 45s), rest 60 to 90s each side
- **Coach sources:** McGill, Dan John

## Turkish Get Up (Light)

`RSH-014 | G1 | Total body: Turkish get up / windmill | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Kettlebell
- **Why we use it:** The get up teaches you to get up from the floor while holding a weight overhead: shoulder stability, hip mobility and confidence in one. Getting off the floor is a key longevity skill (Attia, Dan John, Pavel). Windmills and arm bars build shoulder stability and hip hinge mobility.
- **This variation:** Reduced range/load version: used for rehab, beginners, warm ups or flare up days.
- **Muscles:** Shoulder stability, core, hips, whole body
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Eyes on the bell, arm locked. 2) Move through each step slowly: roll to elbow, hand, high bridge, sweep the leg, kneel, stand. 3) Reverse every step with control.
- **Common faults:** Rushing; Bent arm; Losing sight of the bell.
- **Progress to:** KB Windmill (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Turkish Get Up (G2). **Or progress by:** Heavier bell, full get up.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Half get up, shoe on the fist, no weight.
- **Same level swaps:** Half Turkish Get Up
- **Cautions:** Shoulder. Learn with a shoe or no weight first. Shoulder pain: half get up with no load only.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 5 reps each side, slow
- **Coach sources:** Dan John, Pavel Tsatsouline, Gray Cook

## Isometric External Rotation

`RSH-017 | G1 | Shoulder: isometrics | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Pushing into a wall or band without moving loads the shoulder tendons with almost no irritation. First line for painful rotator cuffs.
- **This variation:** Isometric: builds strength and tendon tolerance in a fixed position with minimal joint irritation.
- **Muscles:** Rotator cuff, deltoid
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Elbow at the side bent to 90 degrees. 2) Push into the wall/band gently and build to about 70%. 3) Hold 30 to 45s, breathe.
- **Common faults:** Shrugging; Pushing to pain; Holding the breath.
- **Progress to:** Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2). **Or progress by:** Longer holds, harder push, move to band rotations.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Lighter push.
- **Same level swaps:** Isometric Internal Rotation; Isometric Shoulder Abduction
- **Cautions:** None specific. Rehab friendly.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 5 x 20 to 45s holds, rest 60s, about 70% effort
- **Coach sources:** Rehab research, Squat University

**Half Kneeling Landmine Press** (G2): full entry under Vertical Push, ID VPU-058.

## Landmine Press (Light)

`RSH-019 | G1 | Push: landmine press | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Landmine (confirm)
- **Why we use it:** The landmine press moves on an arc between a horizontal and vertical press, letting the shoulder blade move freely. It is the most shoulder friendly way to press overhead and the go to for members who can't press straight overhead (Cressey). Half kneeling adds core and hip stability.
- **This variation:** Landmine: the arc path is shoulder and back friendly and very easy to learn. Reduced range/load version: used for rehab, beginners, warm ups or flare up days.
- **Muscles:** Shoulders, chest, triceps, serratus, core
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Hold the end of the bar at the shoulder, ribs down, glutes tight. 2) Press up and forward, letting the shoulder blade reach around. 3) Lower with control back to the shoulder.
- **Common faults:** Arching the low back; Shrugging; Twisting the torso to press.
- **Progress to:** Landmine Press (G2); Landmine Push Press (G2); Landmine Chest Press (G2). **Or progress by:** Half kneeling → tall kneeling → split stance → standing → push press; add plates.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Lighter, two hands, half kneeling.
- **Same level swaps:** Seated DB Shoulder Press
- **Cautions:** None specific. Best press for shoulder pain and limited overhead range.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 (each arm)
- **Coach sources:** Cressey, Boyle, DeFranco

## Side Lying External Rotation (DB)

`RSH-021 | G1 | Shoulder: rotator cuff | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Dumbbells (confirm)
- **Why we use it:** The rotator cuff keeps the ball centred in the socket. Strong external rotators protect the shoulder during pressing (Poliquin's structural balance). Light, frequent and precise.
- **Muscles:** Rotator cuff (infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis)
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Elbow at the side (towel under the arm) or at 90 degrees. 2) Rotate the forearm out slowly. 3) Return with control.
- **Common faults:** Elbow drifting away; Rotating the body; Going heavy.
- **Progress to:** Cross Body Stretch (G2); Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2). **Or progress by:** Side lying DB → cable → 90/90.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Band light, isometric.
- **Same level swaps:** Band External Rotation; Band Internal Rotation; Cable External Rotation
- **Cautions:** None specific. Shoulder rehab friendly. 90/90 versions are harder: progress there.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 12 to 20, slow
- **Coach sources:** Poliquin, Cressey, Squat University

**Lu Raise** (G1): full entry under Vertical Push, ID VPU-027.

## Shrug to Retraction

`RSH-023 | G1 | Shoulder: scapular control | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Training the shoulder blade to move (down, back, up) before the arm pulls. Scapula pull ups and retractions are the first step towards rows and pull ups (G1 of the Optimal row screen).
- **Muscles:** Mid and lower traps, rhomboids, lats
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Arms straight. 2) Move only the shoulder blades. 3) Pause and return.
- **Common faults:** Bending the elbows; Shrugging; Rushing.
- **Progress to:** Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2). **Or progress by:** Full rows/pull ups.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Smaller range.
- **Same level swaps:** Scapula Pull Up; Scapula Retraction (TRX)
- **Cautions:** None specific. Rehab friendly.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8
- **Coach sources:** Squat University, Cressey

## Lower Trap Raise (Prone)

`RSH-025 | G1 | Pull: scapular / lower trap raises | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Small raises in Y, T, W and I shapes strengthen the muscles that control the shoulder blade, especially the lower traps that are often weak in rounded posture. Poliquin's structural balance and Cressey's shoulder programmes rely on them.
- **Muscles:** Lower and middle traps, rear shoulders, rotator cuff
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Chest supported on an incline bench or lying face down. 2) Thumbs up, lift the arms into the shape using the shoulder blades. 3) Pause 1 to 2s at the top, lower slowly.
- **Common faults:** Shrugging up to the ears; Using heavy weights and swinging; Arching the low back.
- **Progress to:** Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2). **Or progress by:** Light DBs, longer pauses.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Bodyweight, smaller range.
- **Same level swaps:** TRX Y Raise; TRX T Raise; TRX W Raise
- **Cautions:** None specific. Shoulder rehab friendly. Use 1 to 3kg or bodyweight.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 8 to 12 per shape, pause at the top
- **Coach sources:** Poliquin, Cressey, Squat University

- **Muscles:** Rotator cuff (infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis)
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Elbow at the side (towel under the arm) or at 90 degrees. 2) Rotate the forearm out slowly. 3) Return with control.
- **Common faults:** Elbow drifting away; Rotating the body; Going heavy.
- **Progress to:** Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2). **Or progress by:** Side lying DB → cable → 90/90.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Band light, isometric.
- **Same level swaps:** Cable External Rotation; External Rotation at 90 Degrees (Cable); Band External Rotation
- **Cautions:** None specific. Shoulder rehab friendly. 90/90 versions are harder: progress there.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 12 to 20, slow
- **Coach sources:** Poliquin, Cressey, Squat University

## Prone Y Raise

`RSH-034 | G1 | Pull: scapular / lower trap raises | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Small raises in Y, T, W and I shapes strengthen the muscles that control the shoulder blade, especially the lower traps that are often weak in rounded posture. Poliquin's structural balance and Cressey's shoulder programmes rely on them.
- **Muscles:** Lower and middle traps, rear shoulders, rotator cuff
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Chest supported on an incline bench or lying face down. 2) Thumbs up, lift the arms into the shape using the shoulder blades. 3) Pause 1 to 2s at the top, lower slowly.
- **Common faults:** Shrugging up to the ears; Using heavy weights and swinging; Arching the low back.
- **Progress to:** Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2). **Or progress by:** Light DBs, longer pauses.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Bodyweight, smaller range.
- **Same level swaps:** TRX Y Raise; TRX T Raise; TRX W Raise
- **Cautions:** None specific. Shoulder rehab friendly. Use 1 to 3kg or bodyweight.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 8 to 12 per shape, pause at the top
- **Coach sources:** Poliquin, Cressey, Squat University
- **Also listed in:** Rehab: Lower Back

## Band Dislocates

`RSH-035 | G1 | Shoulder mobility: gentle range | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Resistance band (confirm)
- **Why we use it:** Gentle shoulder range of motion work. Pendulums and table slides are first stage rehab for stiff or painful shoulders; dowel and band pass throughs maintain overhead and behind body mobility (DeFranco Simple 6).
- **Muscles:** Shoulder joint, capsule, lats, pecs
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Relaxed, no forcing. 2) Move slowly through comfortable range. 3) Breathe.
- **Common faults:** Forcing painful range; Shrugging; Arching to fake range.
- **Progress to:** Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2). **Or progress by:** Bigger range, narrower grip on pass throughs.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Smaller range, table slides.
- **Same level swaps:** Table Slides; Pendulum Swings; Dowel Pass Through
- **Cautions:** None specific. Use pain free range only. Frozen shoulder: refer and follow the physio.
- **Default prescription:** 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down
- **Coach sources:** Squat University, DeFranco (Simple 6), Rehab practice
- **Also listed in:** Mobility And Warm Up

## Prone T Raise

## Thoracic Extension on Foam Roller

`RSH-037 | G1 | Mobility: thoracic spine | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Foam roller (confirm)
- **Why we use it:** The upper back should move; the low back should be stable (joint by joint). Stiff upper backs cause rounded posture, shoulder pain and low back pain, and limit the golf swing. Daily T spine drills fix it.
- **Muscles:** Thoracic spine rotation and extension, lats, pecs
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Keep the hips still (knee pinned or in quadruped). 2) Rotate/extend through the upper back, follow the hand with the eyes. 3) Breathe out into the end range.
- **Common faults:** Rotating from the low back; Rushing; Forcing range.
- **Progress to:** Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2). **Or progress by:** Add a reach, hold end range longer.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Smaller range, seated version.
- **Same level swaps:** Open Book; Thread the Needle; Open Book Stretch
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very safe. Osteoporosis: avoid forced flexion; gentle rotation and extension are fine.
- **Default prescription:** 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down
- **Coach sources:** Squat University, Paul Chek, Cressey
- **Also listed in:** Rehab: Lower Back, Mobility And Warm Up

## Lat Stretch (Bench)

`RSH-042 | G1 | Mobility: stretch / spinal mobility | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Box / bench / step
- **Why we use it:** Static and gentle mobility work restores range lost from sitting and ageing. Best used where a screen shows a restriction (Squat University: screen, correct, retest), and to cool down. McKenzie press ups and extension work often relieve disc type back pain; flexion stretches often suit stenosis type pain: individualise.
- **Muscles:** Target muscles and joints vary (named in the exercise)
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Get into position slowly. 2) Breathe out to relax into range, no bouncing. 3) Hold 30 to 60s or do slow reps.
- **Common faults:** Forcing painful range; Holding the breath; Stretching instead of strengthening when stability is the issue.
- **Progress to:** Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2). **Or progress by:** Longer holds, deeper range, add loaded stretching.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Smaller range, supported versions.
- **Same level swaps:** Frog Stretch; Couch Stretch; Elephant Walk
- **Cautions:** None specific. Gentle and safe. Stop if symptoms travel down the leg. Osteoporosis: avoid loaded flexion stretches.
- **Default prescription:** 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down
- **Coach sources:** Squat University, DeFranco (Limber 11), Ben Patrick (couch stretch), McGill
- **Also listed in:** Mobility And Warm Up

**Band Face Pull** (G1): full entry under Horizontal Pull, ID HPL-022.

**Cable Y Pull** (G2): full entry under Vertical Pull, ID VPL-010.

## Face Pull with External Rotation

`RSH-043 | G1 | Pull: face pull (shoulder health) | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Cable machine
- **Why we use it:** Face pulls combine a high row with external rotation, strengthening the muscles that keep shoulders healthy and posture upright. Cressey and DeFranco use them in almost every programme to balance all the pressing. Optimal: at least 2x per week for desk workers.
- **Muscles:** Rear shoulders, rotator cuff (external rotators), mid traps
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Rope at forehead height, thumbs pointing back. 2) Pull towards the face, elbows high, separate the rope. 3) Finish with the knuckles beside the ears (like a double bicep pose), pause.
- **Common faults:** Leaning back and using bodyweight; Elbows dropping; Shrugging.
- **Progress to:** Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2). **Or progress by:** Heavier, slower, add external rotation emphasis.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Band face pull, lighter.
- **Same level swaps:** TRX Face Pull; Band Face Pull; Cable Face Pull
- **Cautions:** None specific. Shoulder friendly and often therapeutic.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 12 to 20 reps, pause 1s
- **Coach sources:** DeFranco, Cressey, Poliquin (structural balance)

## Shoulder CARs

`RSH-044 | G1 | Mobility: controlled articular rotations (CARs) | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Slow, full range joint circles under tension. Maintains each joint's usable range and gives a daily joint health check.
- **Muscles:** Joint capsule, end range control
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Brace everything else. 2) Move the joint through its biggest circle slowly. 3) Keep tension the whole way.
- **Common faults:** Compensating with other joints; Rushing; Forcing painful range.
- **Progress to:** Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2). **Or progress by:** Bigger circle, more tension.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Smaller circle.
- **Same level swaps:** Hip CARs; Neck CARs; Standing Hip CARs
- **Cautions:** None specific. Universally safe.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 5 slow reps each direction
- **Coach sources:** FRC style mobility, Dean Somerset
- **Also listed in:** Mobility And Warm Up

## Scapula Push Up

`RSH-045 | G1 | Shoulder: serratus anterior | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** The serratus holds the shoulder blade against the ribcage and rotates it upward for overhead reaching. Weak serratus = winging and shoulder pain.
- **Muscles:** Serratus anterior
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Arms straight. 2) Push the floor or weight away, spreading the shoulder blades. 3) Return slowly.
- **Common faults:** Bending the elbows; Shrugging; Sagging hips (push up plus).
- **Progress to:** Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2). **Or progress by:** Push up plus, band punch, heavier.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Wall version.
- **Same level swaps:** Press Up Plus; Serratus Punch (Band); Bear Plank Protraction
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very shoulder friendly.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8
- **Coach sources:** Cressey, Squat University
- **Also listed in:** Mobility And Warm Up

## Hanging (Supported)

`RSH-046 | G2 | Vertical pull: pull up / chin up / hangs | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Check`

- **Equipment:** Rig / pull up bar
- **Why we use it:** The ultimate upper body bodyweight strength test. Hangs build grip (a strong predictor of longevity) and decompress the spine; negatives and isometrics build strength for the first pull up. LIFTMOR used jumping chin ups with drop landings for bone.
- **This variation:** Assisted version: support lets members practise the full pattern safely while strength builds (Cosgrove: regress to progress).
- **Muscles:** Lats, upper back, biceps, grip, core
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Grip slightly wider than shoulders (chin up: palms facing you). 2) Pull the shoulder blades down first, then drive the elbows to the ribs. 3) Chin over the bar, lower slowly to straight arms.
- **Common faults:** Kipping or swinging; Half reps; Shrugging at the bottom.
- **Progress to:** Pull Up (G3); Chin Up (G3); Dead Hang (G3). **Or progress by:** Band assisted → negatives → bodyweight → weighted.
- **Regress to:** Scapula Pull Up (G1); Shrug to Retraction (G1); Scapula Retraction (TRX) (G1). **Or regress by:** Lat pulldown, TRX assisted pull up, scapula pull up, dead hang.
- **Same level swaps:** TRX Assisted Pull Up; Band Assisted Pull Up
- **Cautions:** Shoulder. Shoulder pain: neutral grip, band assistance. Hanging can irritate some shoulders: build up gradually.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 or total reps
- **Coach sources:** DeFranco, Dan John, Attia (grip), Boyle

**Scapula Pull Up** (G1): full entry under Vertical Pull, ID VPL-015.

## Lat Pulldown (Light, Full Range)

`RSH-047 | G1 | Vertical pull: pulldown / pullover | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Cable machine
- **Why we use it:** Pulldowns train the pull up pattern at any load, essential for members who can't yet do pull ups. Straight arm pulldowns and pullovers isolate the lats, which also helps overhead mobility.
- **This variation:** Reduced range/load version: used for rehab, beginners, warm ups or flare up days.
- **Muscles:** Lats, upper back, biceps
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Lean back slightly, chest up. 2) Pull the shoulder blades down then the elbows to the ribs. 3) Return slowly to a full stretch.
- **Common faults:** Leaning way back and rowing; Pulling behind the neck (shoulder risk); Shortening the range.
- **Progress to:** Band Y Pull (G2); Cable Y Pull (G2); Band Pulldown (G2). **Or progress by:** Heavier, single arm, tempo, progress to band assisted pull ups.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Lighter, band pulldown, kneeling.
- **Same level swaps:** Chest Supported DB Row; Chest Supported DB Row (Neutral)
- **Cautions:** None specific. Shoulder friendly with neutral grip. Behind the neck versions: avoid for 40+.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8
- **Coach sources:** Boyle, Poliquin

## Scapula Retraction (TRX)

`RSH-048 | G1 | Shoulder: scapular control | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** TRX
- **Why we use it:** Training the shoulder blade to move (down, back, up) before the arm pulls. Scapula pull ups and retractions are the first step towards rows and pull ups (G1 of the Optimal row screen).
- **Muscles:** Mid and lower traps, rhomboids, lats
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Arms straight. 2) Move only the shoulder blades. 3) Pause and return.
- **Common faults:** Bending the elbows; Shrugging; Rushing.
- **Progress to:** Cable Y Pull (G2); Arm Bar (KB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2). **Or progress by:** Full rows/pull ups.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Smaller range.
- **Same level swaps:** Scapula Pull Up; Shrug to Retraction
- **Cautions:** None specific. Rehab friendly.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8
- **Coach sources:** Squat University, Cressey

## Waiter's Carry (Light)

`RSH-049 | G1 | Carry: overhead / waiter | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Dumbbells (confirm), Kettlebell
- **Why we use it:** Holding weight overhead while walking trains shoulder stability and core in one. Bottoms up holds make the rotator cuff work hard with light weight: brilliant for shoulder rehab.
- **This variation:** Reduced range/load version: used for rehab, beginners, warm ups or flare up days.
- **Muscles:** Shoulder stability, rotator cuff, core
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Arm locked, biceps by the ear, shoulder packed. 2) Ribs down, walk slowly. 3) Keep the weight stacked over the shoulder.
- **Common faults:** Arching the back; Arm drifting forward; Going too heavy.
- **Progress to:** Overhead Hold (DB) (G2); Bottoms Up KB Hold (G2); Overhead Hold (KB) (G2). **Or progress by:** Heavier, double, bottoms up.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Waiter's carry, lighter, static hold.
- **Cautions:** Shoulder. Needs pain free overhead range. Waiter's carry (arm at 90 degrees) is an easier option.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 5 x 20 to 40m (or 30 to 45s), rest 60 to 90s
- **Coach sources:** Dan John, Cressey

## Single Leg Balance (Eyes Closed)

`RHP-001 | G1 | Balance and proprioception | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Balance falls away quickly with age and inactivity; falls are a leading cause of injury in older adults. Single leg balance is part of the Optimal screen. Train it every session for 60+ (Gambetta: postural alignment and dynamic balance are the foundation).
- **Muscles:** Foot, ankle, hip stabilisers, nervous system
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Stand tall near a support. 2) Grip the floor with the foot, soft knee. 3) Hold or reach while keeping the hips level.
- **Common faults:** Locking the knee; Holding the breath; Doing it far from support.
- **Progress to:** Kickstand RDL (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2). **Or progress by:** Eyes closed, cushion, reach, catch a ball.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Hand on support, tandem stance.
- **Same level swaps:** Heel to Toe Walk; Single Leg Balance; Tandem Stance Balance
- **Cautions:** None specific. Always near a rail or rig for seniors.
- **Default prescription:** 3 x 20 to 30s each leg
- **Coach sources:** Gambetta, Falls prevention research

**Single Leg Glute Bridge** (G2): full entry under Hinge Pattern: Unilateral, ID HGU-037.

`RHP-002 | G1 | Balance and proprioception | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

## Clam Shell

`RHP-004 | G1 | Hip: abduction / glute med | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** The side glutes stop the knee caving and the pelvis dropping when on one leg. Weak glute meds are linked to knee pain, hip pain and back pain. Simple band work fixes it and works brilliantly as a warm up (Squat University, Boyle).
- **Muscles:** Glute medius and minimus, hip stabilisers
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Athletic stance, band around the knees or ankles. 2) Push the knees out, step sideways (or lift the leg) leading with the heel. 3) Stay low and keep the pelvis level.
- **Common faults:** Rocking the torso side to side; Feet turning out; Letting the band pull the knees in.
- **Progress to:** Cossack Squat (G2); Paused Hip Thrust (G2); Lateral Lunge (DB) (G2). **Or progress by:** Heavier band, band lower on the leg, side plank abduction.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Side lying with no band, smaller range.
- **Same level swaps:** Monster Walk; Reverse Clam; Fire Hydrant
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very joint friendly, ideal for hip and knee rehab.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 20 each side
- **Coach sources:** Squat University, Boyle, Paul Chek

## Step Up (Low Box)

`RHP-005 | G2 | Single leg: step up | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Box / bench / step
- **Why we use it:** A real life movement (stairs, kerbs, climbing). Very back friendly, easy to scale by box height, and the concentric emphasis means little soreness. Knee drive and crossover versions add balance and hip work.
- **Muscles:** Quads, glutes, hamstrings, balance
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Whole foot on the box, knee over the middle of the foot. 2) Lean forward slightly and drive through the box leg to stand tall. 3) Step down with control, don't push off the bottom leg.
- **Common faults:** Pushing off the floor leg; Knee caving as you stand; Box too high so the hip hikes.
- **Progress to:** Barbell Step Up (G3); Step Up to Single Leg RDL (G3). **Or progress by:** Higher box, add DBs/goblet/barbell, add a knee drive, slower lowering.
- **Regress to:** Patrick Step (G1); Poliquin Step Up (G1); Petersen Step Up (G1). **Or regress by:** Lower box, hand support, bodyweight.
- **Same level swaps:** DB Step Up; Goblet Step Up; Lateral Step Up
- **Cautions:** None specific. Knee friendly at lower heights. Use a low box and hand support for seniors and knee pain. Faster 'step ups' in BURN keep impact low.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 (each leg)
- **Coach sources:** Boyle, Cosgrove, Gambetta
- **Also listed in:** Rehab: Knee

## Single Leg RDL (Supported)

`RHP-007 | G2 | Hinge: single leg / staggered | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Single leg hinges build hamstring and glute strength, balance and hip stability one side at a time, and they spare the spine because loads are lighter. Kickstand and B stance versions give a stepping stone with the back foot for support. Hip airplanes train hip rotation control (great for golf).
- **This variation:** Assisted version: support lets members practise the full pattern safely while strength builds (Cosgrove: regress to progress).
- **Muscles:** Hamstrings, glutes (incl. glute med), foot and ankle stability
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Stand on one leg with a soft knee, other leg reaching back. 2) Hinge forward as one straight line from head to heel, hips square. 3) Drive the standing heel into the floor and squeeze the glute to stand.
- **Common faults:** Hips opening up (rotating) towards the ceiling; Rounding the back to reach the floor; Standing knee locked straight.
- **Progress to:** TRX Single Leg RDL (G3); Single Leg RDL (DB) (G3); Single Leg RDL (KB) (G3). **Or progress by:** Kickstand → full single leg, add load (DB/KB, double KB, landmine), slower tempo, add a row or reach.
- **Regress to:** KB Deadlift (G1); DB Deadlift (G1); Sumo KB Deadlift (G1). **Or regress by:** Supported single leg RDL (hand on rig), kickstand RDL, bodyweight.
- **Same level swaps:** Kickstand RDL; Banded Airplane; Kickstand RDL (DB)
- **Cautions:** None specific. Back friendly. Balance limits load: use a support or kickstand first. Excellent for golfers and runners.
- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9 (each leg)
- **Coach sources:** Boyle, Cosgrove, Gambetta

**Side Lying Hip Abduction** (G1): full entry under Lateral Movements, ID LAT-033.

## Split Squat (Supported)

`RHP-011 | G1 | Single leg: split squat | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** The entry point of the single leg ladder. A static split stance gives a stable base, so people learn to load one leg at a time safely. It builds balance, fixes imbalances and is far easier on the back than heavy bilateral squats. Front foot elevated adds knee travel (ATG style); cable and landmine versions add stability.
- **This variation:** Assisted version: support lets members practise the full pattern safely while strength builds (Cosgrove: regress to progress).
- **Muscles:** Quads, glutes, adductors
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Long split stance, both feet pointing forward, hip width apart. 2) Lower the back knee straight down towards the floor. 3) Push through the front foot to stand, keep the torso tall.
- **Common faults:** Stance too narrow (tightrope), losing balance; Front heel lifting; Lunging forward instead of dropping down.
- **Progress to:** ATG Split Squat (G2); SSB Split Squat (G2); Split Squat (DB) (G2). **Or progress by:** Add load, elevate the front foot (ATG style), then elevate the back foot (RFESS).
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** TRX or rig assisted split squat, shorter range, isometric split squat hold.
- **Same level swaps:** Split Squat (Bodyweight); TRX Assisted Split Squat; Split Squat (Short Range)
- **Cautions:** None specific. Knee friendly when depth is controlled. Use a pad under the back knee. Hold a support for balance in seniors.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 4 sets x 6 to 10 reps, tempo 3-1-1-0, rest 90 to 120s, RPE 7 to 8 (each leg)
- **Coach sources:** Boyle, Squat University, Ben Patrick (front foot elevated)

## Donkey Kick

`RHP-012 | G1 | Hinge: hip extension accessory | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Cable/band pull throughs teach the hip hinge with the load pulling from behind, so people naturally sit the hips back and finish with the glutes. Kickbacks and quadruped hip extensions isolate the glutes for activation and rehab.
- **Muscles:** Glutes, hamstrings
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Face away from the cable, rope between the legs. 2) Hinge back letting the rope pull the hips back. 3) Drive the hips through and squeeze the glutes, stand tall.
- **Common faults:** Pulling with the arms; Squatting instead of hinging; Leaning back at the top.
- **Progress to:** KB Swings (G2); KB Swing (Power) (G2); American KB Swing (G2). **Or progress by:** Heavier, pause at the top, progress to KB swing.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Band version, shorter range.
- **Same level swaps:** Cable Kickback; Band Pull Through; Cable Pull Through
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very back friendly. A great swing and deadlift regression.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8
- **Coach sources:** Cosgrove, McGill, Boyle

**Frog Pump** (G1): full entry under Hinge Pattern: Bilateral, ID HGB-028.

## Hip Flexor March (Supine)

`RHP-013 | G1 | Hip: hip flexor strength | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Hip flexor strength (especially lifting the knee above 90 degrees) declines with age and affects walking, stairs and tripping. Ben Patrick includes it in ATG Zero.
- **Muscles:** Hip flexors (psoas, rectus femoris)
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Sit or lie tall. 2) Lift the knee up without leaning back. 3) Lower slowly.
- **Common faults:** Leaning back; Arching the low back; Momentum.
- **Progress to:** Kickstand RDL (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2). **Or progress by:** Band resistance, standing, longer holds.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Smaller range.
- **Same level swaps:** Psoas March (Standing); Banded Hip Flexor March; Standing Cable Hip Flexion
- **Cautions:** None specific. Gentle and safe. Hip impingement: keep below pain.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8
- **Coach sources:** Ben Patrick (ATG), Rehab practice

## Hip Thrust (Paused)

`RHP-014 | G2 | Hinge: hip extension (bridge / thrust) | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Box / bench / step
- **Why we use it:** Bridges and hip thrusts train the glutes at their strongest point (full hip extension) with almost no spinal load. They are essential for back pain, knee pain, posture, sprinting and golf power, and are safe for nearly everyone. Single leg versions fix imbalances.
- **This variation:** Paused version: holding the hardest position removes the bounce and builds strength exactly where people usually fail.
- **Muscles:** Glutes, hamstrings
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Feet flat, shins vertical at the top. 2) Tuck the ribs down, drive through the heels and squeeze the glutes to lift. 3) Pause at the top without arching the low back, lower slowly.
- **Common faults:** Arching the low back instead of extending the hips; Feet too far away (all hamstrings); Pushing through the toes.
- **Progress to:** Nordic Curl (Full) (G3); Slider Hamstring Curl (G3); Hamstring Curl (Slider) (G3). **Or progress by:** Bridge → hip thrust off a bench → load (DB, barbell) → single leg, add pauses or bands.
- **Regress to:** Frog Pump (G1); Glute Bridge (G1); Hip Thrust (DB) (G1). **Or regress by:** Floor bridge, shorter range, isometric hold.
- **Same level swaps:** Paused Hip Thrust; Barbell Hip Thrust; Barbell Glute Bridge
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very joint friendly. Use a pad on the hips when loaded. Shoulder elevated versions need a stable bench.
- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9 (pause 1 to 2s at the top)
- **Coach sources:** Cosgrove, McGill, Boyle

## Banded Hip Flexor March

`RHP-015 | G1 | Hip: hip flexor strength | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Resistance band (confirm)
- **Why we use it:** Hip flexor strength (especially lifting the knee above 90 degrees) declines with age and affects walking, stairs and tripping. Ben Patrick includes it in ATG Zero.
- **This variation:** Band resistance gets harder at the top (accommodating resistance) and can cue better positions such as knees out.
- **Muscles:** Hip flexors (psoas, rectus femoris)
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Sit or lie tall. 2) Lift the knee up without leaning back. 3) Lower slowly.
- **Common faults:** Leaning back; Arching the low back; Momentum.
- **Progress to:** Kickstand RDL (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2). **Or progress by:** Band resistance, standing, longer holds.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Smaller range.
- **Same level swaps:** Psoas March (Standing); Hip Flexor March (Supine); Standing Cable Hip Flexion
- **Cautions:** None specific. Gentle and safe. Hip impingement: keep below pain.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8
- **Coach sources:** Ben Patrick (ATG), Rehab practice

## Couch Stretch

`RHP-016 | G1 | Mobility: stretch / spinal mobility | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Static and gentle mobility work restores range lost from sitting and ageing. Best used where a screen shows a restriction (Squat University: screen, correct, retest), and to cool down. McKenzie press ups and extension work often relieve disc type back pain; flexion stretches often suit stenosis type pain: individualise.
- **Muscles:** Target muscles and joints vary (named in the exercise)
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Get into position slowly. 2) Breathe out to relax into range, no bouncing. 3) Hold 30 to 60s or do slow reps.
- **Common faults:** Forcing painful range; Holding the breath; Stretching instead of strengthening when stability is the issue.
- **Progress to:** Kickstand RDL (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2). **Or progress by:** Longer holds, deeper range, add loaded stretching.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Smaller range, supported versions.
- **Same level swaps:** Frog Stretch; Elephant Walk; Pigeon Stretch
- **Cautions:** None specific. Gentle and safe. Stop if symptoms travel down the leg. Osteoporosis: avoid loaded flexion stretches.
- **Default prescription:** 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down
- **Coach sources:** Squat University, DeFranco (Limber 11), Ben Patrick (couch stretch), McGill
- **Also listed in:** Rehab: Knee, Rehab: Lower Back, Mobility And Warm Up

McKenzie press ups and extension work often relieve disc type back pain; flexion stretches often suit stenosis type pain: individualise.
- **This variation:** Kneeling position locks the hips so the core has to control the trunk and stops the legs cheating.
- **Muscles:** Target muscles and joints vary (named in the exercise)
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Get into position slowly. 2) Breathe out to relax into range, no bouncing. 3) Hold 30 to 60s or do slow reps.
- **Common faults:** Forcing painful range; Holding the breath; Stretching instead of strengthening when stability is the issue.
- **Progress to:** Kickstand RDL (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2). **Or progress by:** Longer holds, deeper range, add loaded stretching.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Smaller range, supported versions.
- **Same level swaps:** Frog Stretch; Couch Stretch; Elephant Walk
- **Cautions:** None specific. Gentle and safe. Stop if symptoms travel down the leg. Osteoporosis: avoid loaded flexion stretches.
- **Default prescription:** 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down
- **Coach sources:** Squat University, DeFranco (Limber 11), Ben Patrick (couch stretch), McGill
- **Also listed in:** Rehab: Lower Back, Mobility And Warm Up

## Seated Knee Raise (Hip Flexor)

`RHP-019 | G1 | Hip: hip flexor strength | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Hip flexor strength (especially lifting the knee above 90 degrees) declines with age and affects walking, stairs and tripping. Ben Patrick includes it in ATG Zero.
- **Muscles:** Hip flexors (psoas, rectus femoris)
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Sit or lie tall. 2) Lift the knee up without leaning back. 3) Lower slowly.
- **Common faults:** Leaning back; Arching the low back; Momentum.
- **Progress to:** Kickstand RDL (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2). **Or progress by:** Band resistance, standing, longer holds.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Smaller range.
- **Same level swaps:** Psoas March (Standing); Banded Hip Flexor March; Hip Flexor March (Supine)
- **Cautions:** None specific. Gentle and safe. Hip impingement: keep below pain.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8
- **Coach sources:** Ben Patrick (ATG), Rehab practice

## Standing Hip CARs

`RHP-021 | G1 | Mobility: controlled articular rotations (CARs) | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Slow, full range joint circles under tension. Maintains each joint's usable range and gives a daily joint health check.
- **Muscles:** Joint capsule, end range control
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Brace everything else. 2) Move the joint through its biggest circle slowly. 3) Keep tension the whole way.
- **Common faults:** Compensating with other joints; Rushing; Forcing painful range.
- **Progress to:** Kickstand RDL (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2). **Or progress by:** Bigger circle, more tension.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Smaller circle.
- **Same level swaps:** Hip CARs; Neck CARs; Shoulder CARs
- **Cautions:** None specific. Universally safe.
- **Default prescription:** 3 to 5 slow reps each direction
- **Coach sources:** FRC style mobility, Dean Somerset

## Adductor Rock Back

`RHP-024 | G1 | Mobility: spinal / back care | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Gentle spinal mobility for back care and warm ups. Extension drills (prone lying, McKenzie press ups) often ease disc type back pain; flexion drills (knee to chest, child's pose) often ease stiffness and stenosis type pain. Find the direction that helps the individual (McGill: find the pain triggers) and use it.
- **Muscles:** Spine, hips
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Move slowly through comfortable range. 2) Breathe out into the end range. 3) Stop if symptoms travel down a leg.
- **Common faults:** Forcing range; Holding the breath; Bouncing.
- **Progress to:** Kickstand RDL (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2). **Or progress by:** Bigger range, add breathing holds.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Smaller range.
- **Same level swaps:** Cat Cow; Child's Pose; Supine Twist
- **Cautions:** None specific. Generally very safe. Osteoporosis: avoid repeated or loaded spinal flexion. Pain spreading into a leg: stop and refer.
- **Default prescription:** 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down
- **Coach sources:** McGill, Squat University, McKenzie method (physio)

## 90/90 Hip Switch

`RHP-025 | G1 | Hip: rotation mobility | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Hip internal and external rotation are often the first ranges lost with age and are critical for the golf swing, squat depth and low back health (joint by joint).
- **Muscles:** Hip rotators, capsule
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Sit tall in 90/90 or lie in position. 2) Rotate through the hips, keep the chest tall. 3) Move slowly, hold the end range.
- **Common faults:** Rounding the back; Forcing; Using hands to cheat.
- **Progress to:** Kickstand RDL (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2). **Or progress by:** Hands free, hip lifts, longer holds.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Hands support.
- **Same level swaps:** Shin Box; 90/90 Hip Lift; Shin Box Get Up
- **Cautions:** None specific. Hip pain: reduce range.
- **Default prescription:** 1 to 2 sets x 5 to 10 slow reps (or 30 to 60s), in warm up or cool down
- **Coach sources:** Squat University, Gambetta (golf)
- **Also listed in:** Mobility And Warm Up

## Hip Airplane (Supported)

`RHP-029 | G1 | Hinge: single leg / staggered | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Single leg hinges build hamstring and glute strength, balance and hip stability one side at a time, and they spare the spine because loads are lighter. Kickstand and B stance versions give a stepping stone with the back foot for support. Hip airplanes train hip rotation control (great for golf).
- **This variation:** Assisted version: support lets members practise the full pattern safely while strength builds (Cosgrove: regress to progress).
- **Muscles:** Hamstrings, glutes (incl. glute med), foot and ankle stability
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Stand on one leg with a soft knee, other leg reaching back. 2) Hinge forward as one straight line from head to heel, hips square. 3) Drive the standing heel into the floor and squeeze the glute to stand.
- **Common faults:** Hips opening up (rotating) towards the ceiling; Rounding the back to reach the floor; Standing knee locked straight.
- **Progress to:** Kickstand RDL (G2); Banded Airplane (G2); Kickstand RDL (DB) (G2). **Or progress by:** Kickstand → full single leg, add load (DB/KB, double KB, landmine), slower tempo, add a row or reach.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Supported single leg RDL (hand on rig), kickstand RDL, bodyweight.
- **Same level swaps:** KB Deadlift; DB Deadlift; Sumo KB Deadlift
- **Cautions:** None specific. Back friendly. Balance limits load: use a support or kickstand first. Excellent for golfers and runners.
- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9 (each leg)
- **Coach sources:** Boyle, Cosgrove, Gambetta
- **Also listed in:** Rehab: Lower Back

## Isometric Hip Abduction (Wall)

`RHP-031 | G1 | Hip: abduction / glute med | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** The side glutes stop the knee caving and the pelvis dropping when on one leg. Weak glute meds are linked to knee pain, hip pain and back pain. Simple band work fixes it and works brilliantly as a warm up (Squat University, Boyle).
- **This variation:** Isometric: builds strength and tendon tolerance in a fixed position with minimal joint irritation.
- **Muscles:** Glute medius and minimus, hip stabilisers
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Athletic stance, band around the knees or ankles. 2) Push the knees out, step sideways (or lift the leg) leading with the heel. 3) Stay low and keep the pelvis level.
- **Common faults:** Rocking the torso side to side; Feet turning out; Letting the band pull the knees in.
- **Progress to:** Cossack Squat (G2); Paused Hip Thrust (G2); Lateral Lunge (DB) (G2). **Or progress by:** Heavier band, band lower on the leg, side plank abduction.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Side lying with no band, smaller range.
- **Same level swaps:** Clam Shell; Monster Walk; Reverse Clam
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very joint friendly, ideal for hip and knee rehab.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 20 each side
- **Coach sources:** Squat University, Boyle, Paul Chek

## Isometric Adductor Squeeze (Ball)

`RHP-033 | G2 | Hip: adductor strength | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Copenhagen planks are among the best researched ways to prevent groin injury, and adductor strength supports knee and hip health. Ball squeezes are a gentle entry point.
- **This variation:** Isometric: builds strength and tendon tolerance in a fixed position with minimal joint irritation.
- **Muscles:** Adductors (inner thigh), core
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Side plank with the top leg on a bench (inside of the knee for short lever, ankle for long lever). 2) Lift the hips into a straight line by squeezing the top leg down. 3) Hold or lift and lower.
- **Common faults:** Hips sagging; Rolling forward; Starting with the long lever.
- **Progress to:** Adductor Slide (Slider) (G3); Copenhagen Plank (Long Lever) (G3). **Or progress by:** Short → long lever, add leg raises.
- **Regress to:** Shin Box (G1); Box Squat (G1); Frog Pump (G1). **Or regress by:** Ball squeeze, side lying adduction.
- **Same level swaps:** Copenhagen Side Plank; Adductor Squeeze (Ball); Side Lying Hip Adduction
- **Cautions:** None specific. Short lever first. Groin pain: ball squeeze isometrics.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 15 to 30s each side
- **Coach sources:** Research (groin injury prevention), Boyle

## Side Plank Hip Abduction

`RHP-036 | G2 | Core: anti lateral flexion (side plank) | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Part of the McGill Big 3. Builds the side core that stabilises the spine when carrying or standing on one leg. Hip abduction versions also train the glute med.
- **Muscles:** Obliques, quadratus lumborum, glute med
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Elbow under the shoulder, body in a straight line. 2) Push the hips up and forward. 3) Breathe and hold.
- **Common faults:** Hips sagging or piking back; Rolling forward; Shoulder shrugging.
- **Progress to:** Adductor Slide (Slider) (G3); Uneven Front Rack Carry (G3); Copenhagen Plank (Long Lever) (G3). **Or progress by:** Feet stacked, add hip abduction, Copenhagen.
- **Regress to:** Side Plank (Knees) (G1); Copenhagen Plank (Short Lever) (G1). **Or regress by:** Knees bent side plank.
- **Same level swaps:** Side Plank; Side Plank Clam; Side Plank Hip Dips
- **Cautions:** None specific. Shoulder pain: kneeling version or suitcase carry instead.
- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 15 to 45s each side (or 6/4/2 x 10s)
- **Coach sources:** McGill, Squat University

**Monster Walk** (G1): full entry under Lateral Movements, ID LAT-029.

## Cossack Squat (Assisted)

`RHP-039 | G1 | Single leg: lateral (frontal plane) | HYBRID, STRONG, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Most training is forwards and backwards; lateral lunges train the side to side plane, building adductor strength and hip mobility that protect against groin strains and help golf, tennis and walking on uneven ground. Cossack squats are a great mobility and strength hybrid (Squat University and DeFranco's Limber 11).
- **This variation:** Assisted version: support lets members practise the full pattern safely while strength builds (Cosgrove: regress to progress).
- **Muscles:** Adductors, glutes, quads, hip mobility
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Step wide to the side, toes forward or slightly out. 2) Sit back into one hip, keeping the other leg straight. 3) Push back to the start through the bent leg.
- **Common faults:** Knee caving on the bent leg; Rounding the back to get lower; Heel lifting.
- **Progress to:** Cossack Squat (G2); Lateral Lunge (DB) (G2); Cable Lateral Lunge (G2). **Or progress by:** Add load (goblet, DB, landmine), slider, deeper cossack.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Shorter range, hand support, lateral lunge rock (mobility).
- **Same level swaps:** Clam Shell; Monster Walk; Reverse Clam
- **Cautions:** None specific. Groin and hip sensitive members: reduce range. Assisted versions (holding the rig) for seniors.
- **Default prescription:** 3 sets x 8 to 12 reps, tempo 3-0-1-1, rest 60 to 90s, RPE 7 to 9 (each side)
- **Coach sources:** Gambetta (multi plane), DeFranco (Limber 11), Squat University

**Standing Cable Hip Abduction** (G1): full entry under Lateral Movements, ID LAT-049.

## Hip Hike (Step)

`RHP-040 | G1 | Hip: abduction / glute med | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** The side glutes stop the knee caving and the pelvis dropping when on one leg. Weak glute meds are linked to knee pain, hip pain and back pain. Simple band work fixes it and works brilliantly as a warm up (Squat University, Boyle).
- **Muscles:** Glute medius and minimus, hip stabilisers
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Athletic stance, band around the knees or ankles. 2) Push the knees out, step sideways (or lift the leg) leading with the heel. 3) Stay low and keep the pelvis level.
- **Common faults:** Rocking the torso side to side; Feet turning out; Letting the band pull the knees in.
- **Progress to:** Cossack Squat (G2); Paused Hip Thrust (G2); Lateral Lunge (DB) (G2). **Or progress by:** Heavier band, band lower on the leg, side plank abduction.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Side lying with no band, smaller range.
- **Same level swaps:** Clam Shell; Monster Walk; Reverse Clam
- **Cautions:** None specific. Very joint friendly, ideal for hip and knee rehab.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 20 each side
- **Coach sources:** Squat University, Boyle, Paul Chek

**Standing Cable Hip Extension** (G1): full entry under Hinge Pattern: Unilateral, ID HGU-060.

## Seated Band Hip Abduction

`RHP-041 | G1 | Hip: abduction / glute med | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Resistance band (confirm)
- **Why we use it:** The side glutes stop the knee caving and the pelvis dropping when on one leg. Weak glute meds are linked to knee pain, hip pain and back pain. Simple band work fixes it and works brilliantly as a warm up (Squat University, Boyle).

## Standing Cable Hip Flexion

`RHP-042 | G1 | Hip: hip flexor strength | STRONG, HYBRID | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Cable machine
- **Why we use it:** Hip flexor strength (especially lifting the knee above 90 degrees) declines with age and affects walking, stairs and tripping. Ben Patrick includes it in ATG Zero.
- **This variation:** Cable: constant tension through the whole range with smooth, joint friendly resistance.
- **Muscles:** Hip flexors (psoas, rectus femoris)
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Sit or lie tall. 2) Lift the knee up without leaning back. 3) Lower slowly.
- **Common faults:** Leaning back; Arching the low back; Momentum.
- **Progress to:** Kickstand RDL (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2). **Or progress by:** Band resistance, standing, longer holds.
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Smaller range.
- **Same level swaps:** Psoas March (Standing); Banded Hip Flexor March; Hip Flexor March (Supine)
- **Cautions:** None specific. Gentle and safe. Hip impingement: keep below pain.
- **Default prescription:** 2 to 3 sets x 10 to 15 reps, tempo 2-1-1-1, rest 45 to 60s, RPE 8
- **Coach sources:** Ben Patrick (ATG), Rehab practice

## Pelvic Tilt (Supine)

`RHP-043 | G1 | Core: breathing and pelvic control | STRONG, HYBRID, BURN | Group: Yes | Impact: none | Teams only: No | Seniors: Yes`

- **Equipment:** Bodyweight
- **Why we use it:** Breathing is the foundation of bracing (Chek: breathing first). Crocodile and 90/90 breathing teach 360 degree breathing, calm the nervous system and help back pain and pelvic floor function.
- **Muscles:** Diaphragm, deep core, pelvic floor
- **Coaching cues:** 1) Lie in position, hands on the lower ribs. 2) Breathe in through the nose expanding 360 degrees (belly, sides, back). 3) Exhale slowly fully, feeling the ribs drop.
- **Common faults:** Chest and shoulder breathing; Arching the back; Rushing.
- **Progress to:** Kickstand RDL (G2); Lateral Step Down (G2); Step Up (Low Box) (G2). **Or progress by:** Add movement (dead bug with breathing).
- **Regress to:** None named, use the levers. **Or regress by:** Shorter sets.
- **Same level swaps:** Pelvic Tilt; 90/90 Breathing; 4 Point TVA Draw In (Chek)
- **Cautions:** None specific. Universally safe. Great on RED readiness days.
- **Default prescription:** 5 to 10 slow breaths
- **Coach sources:** Paul Chek, McGill, Squat University
